lessons.title: Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto's Government (1971-77)
lessons.notes_html:
On 16th December, 1971, Dhaka fell due to internal strife and direct military intervention of India. East Pakistan was separated and emerged as Bangladesh. General Yahya Khan resigned and on 20th December, 1971 transferred power to Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto as Chief Martial Law Administrator. Bhutto, who was foreign minister at that time, forced the Army chief to resign and appointed General Tikka Khan as the new Commander-in-Chief. He strengthened relations with Muslim countries and the international community, signed the Simla Agreement with India (India released all prisoners of war), and in April, 1972 lifted martial law and restored democracy.

Economic Reforms: Agricultural Reforms

Bhutto promulgated the Agricultural Reforms Ordinance on 1st March, 1972:

  • Land possession limit reduced from 500 to 150 acres of canal irrigated land, and from 1000 to 300 acres of rainfed land.
  • Tenants would have Haq-e-Shufa'a if the land they cultivate is sold by its owner.
  • No one could evict the tenants, except when the share of produce has not been paid to the landlord.
  • Owners shall supply seeds and pay land revenue and irrigation water charges.
  • Land above the limit shall be confiscated and divided among the tenants, free of cost.
  • A civil servant, during service or after retirement, can possess only 100 acres of land.
  • State agricultural lands shall be divided among landless farmers.

Reforms for Industrial Workers

To fulfil his slogan "bread, cloth and house for everyone", Bhutto introduced Labour Reforms — permission for Trade Union activities and job security:

  • Labour Courts (special courts) were set up to protect workers' rights.
  • 5% share for labour in the total profit of the industry was made obligatory as bonus.
  • Medical facility for industrial workers was made obligatory.
  • Group Insurance and Social Security were introduced — compensation to the labour's family in case of injury or death during service.
  • Owners of big enterprises were bound to bear educational expenses of at least one child of every labour up to matric level.

Devaluation of Rupee

On 11th May, 1972, the Bhutto Government devalued the Pakistani rupee against foreign currencies, especially the US dollar, to encourage exports.

Nationalization Policy

  • Industries: On 2nd January, 1972, Bhutto announced taking big industrial units under state control. It aimed to protect public interests but produced negative results: private investment declined, capitalists shifted capital abroad, and due to mismanagement and labour unions the nationalized industries suffered heavy losses and production fell.
  • Insurance Companies: All insurance companies were nationalised and merged into the State Life Insurance Corporation, later divided into groups to create competition.
  • Banks: On 1st January, 1974, all banks were nationalised under the State Bank of Pakistan. The government got effective control over the flow of capital, but bank performance declined due to non-cooperative unions of bank employees.

Educational Reforms

Bhutto announced his educational policy on 15th March, 1972:

  • From 1st October 1972 and 1st October 1974, education shall be free up to level 8 and 10 respectively.
  • All private schools and colleges were nationalized; no appointment in them without government approval.
  • Stipends and interest-free loans shall be provided to students.

Impacts of Bhutto's Government Reforms

Instead of bringing good, the reforms added to the people's miseries. Industrial reforms created tussles between industrialists and labours; production declined as labours gave up commitment and got involved in unionist activities; industrialists suffered losses and shut down factories; low production dropped exports and affected foreign trade. Due to nationalization of educational institutions, the standard of education suffered, discipline fell, and students got involved in practical politics, which badly affected the educational environment.

Constitution 1973

On 17th April, 1972, the National Assembly formed a Constitutional Committee of twenty-five members from all political parties. The committee presented its draft on 2nd February, 1973; the Assembly approved it on 10th April, 1973. After endorsement by the President on 12th April, the constitution was enacted on 14th August, 1973. Chaudhry Fazal Elahi was elected President and Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto took oath as Prime Minister. Salient features:

  • Written Constitution: It exists in written form and comprises 280 articles.
  • Islamic Provisions: The Objectives Resolution (March, 1949) was made a substantive part; sovereignty over the universe belongs to Allah Almighty; the state shall exercise authority through democratically elected representatives; Islam is the state religion; the president and prime minister must be Muslims.
  • Parliamentary System: The National Assembly elects the prime minister, who is chief executive and accountable to the National Assembly.
  • Federal Constitution: Pakistan is a federal republic; power sharing between federation and provinces is well defined.
  • Free Judiciary: The constitution secures the independence of the Judiciary.
  • Rule of Law: All citizens are accountable before the law irrespective of ethnicity, language or designation.
  • Fundamental Rights: Fundamental rights are ensured to all citizens irrespective of religion or ethnicity; rights of minorities are also guaranteed.
  • National Language: Urdu is the national language; steps shall be taken to make it the official language within 15 years; till then English shall continue as official language.
  • High Treason: Whoever abrogates the constitution by unconstitutional means, or attempts to do so, shall be guilty of High Treason.

Key Points

  • Bhutto took power on 20th December, 1971 after the fall of Dhaka and separation of East Pakistan.
  • Agricultural Reforms Ordinance (1st March, 1972) fixed land limits at 150 acres irrigated and 300 acres rainfed.
  • Labour Reforms gave trade union rights, Labour Courts and a 5% profit share as bonus.
  • Industries, insurance companies and banks (1st January, 1974) were nationalized, but production and performance declined.
  • The 1973 Constitution — written, Islamic, parliamentary and federal — was enacted on 14th August, 1973.

mcqs.q: When did Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto take over power in Pakistan?
mcqs.why: After the fall of Dhaka on 16th December 1971, General Yahya Khan resigned and transferred power to Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto on 20th December, 1971, as Chief Martial Law Administrator.

mcqs.q: Under the Agricultural Reforms Ordinance of 1st March 1972, the land possession limit for canal irrigated land was reduced to:
mcqs.why: The ordinance reduced the limit from 500 to 150 acres of canal irrigated land, and from 1000 to 300 acres of rainfed land; land above the limit was confiscated and divided among tenants free of cost.

mcqs.q: What right did the Agricultural Reforms give to tenants if the land they cultivated was sold by its owner?
options: Right to stop paying the produce share
Right to sell the land himself
mcqs.why: The reforms gave tenants Haq-e-Shufa'a if the land they cultivated was sold by its owner, and no one could evict them except when the share of produce had not been paid to the landlord.

mcqs.q: Under Bhutto's Labour Reforms, what share of the industry's total profit was made obligatory for labour as bonus?
mcqs.why: The Labour Reforms made a 5% share for labour in the total profit of the industry obligatory as bonus, along with Labour Courts, medical facilities, group insurance and social security.

mcqs.q: Why did the Bhutto Government devalue the Pakistani rupee on 11th May, 1972?
options: To increase the price of foreign goods in Pakistan
To reduce the value of the US dollar
mcqs.why: The rupee was devalued against foreign currencies, especially the US dollar, to encourage exports, because cheaper Pakistani goods could compete better in foreign markets.

mcqs.q: When were all banks in Pakistan nationalised?
mcqs.why: All banks were nationalised on 1st January, 1974 under the State Bank of Pakistan; big industries had been taken over on 2nd January, 1972 and insurance companies were merged into the State Life Insurance Corporation.

mcqs.q: According to Bhutto's educational policy of 15th March 1972, education was to be free up to class 8 from:
mcqs.why: The policy announced that from 1st October 1972 education would be free up to level 8, and from 1st October 1974 up to level 10; all private schools and colleges were also nationalized.

mcqs.q: On which date was the Constitution of 1973 enacted?
mcqs.why: The Assembly approved the draft on 10th April 1973, the President endorsed it on 12th April, and the constitution was enacted on 14th August, 1973, after which Bhutto took oath as Prime Minister.

mcqs.q: How many articles does the Constitution of 1973 comprise?
mcqs.why: The 1973 Constitution is a written constitution comprising 280 articles; it is Islamic, parliamentary and federal, and makes the Objectives Resolution of March 1949 a substantive part of it.

mcqs.q: Under the 1973 Constitution, within how many years were steps to be taken to make Urdu the official language?
mcqs.why: The constitution declares Urdu the national language and says steps shall be taken to make it the official language within 15 years; till then English continues as the official language.

lessons.title: Zia-ul-Haq's Government (1977-88)
lessons.notes_html:
In March, 1977, the Pakistan National Alliance (PNA) launched a movement against the government on the charge of rigging the elections. The agitation turned violent, so the Chief of Army Staff, General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq, sacked Bhutto's Government on 5th July, 1977 and imposed Martial Law. General Zia resolved to hold free and fair elections in October the same year, but instead formed his cabinet in August 1978 and designated himself President of Pakistan. He remained in power for more than eleven years.

Measures for Islamisation

  • Introduced "prayer break" in government offices during work hours.
  • At the start of Ramadan-ul-Mubarak on 14th August, 1978, announced measures for the sanctity of the month: ban on eating, drinking and smoking publicly, and closing cinema houses during Taraweeh prayers.
  • On 13th August, 1984, issued directives to establish the prayer system; Prayer Monitors (Nazimeen-e-Salat) were appointed.
  • Pakistan Television was given the task to produce and telecast special religious programmes.
  • Ordered to start every official letter with Bismillah-ir-Rahman-ir-Rahim.
  • Took steps to improve Hajj facilities; a Hajj Conference was held every year to discuss Hajj affairs.
  • Promulgated the Hadood Ordinance — the most important step — enforcing the four punishments clearly enshrined in the Holy Quran: for theft, adultery, wine drinking and false accusation of adultery.
  • On 15th June, 1988, issued the Shariah Ordinance, declaring Islamic Shariah the supreme law of the country.
  • The Zakat and Ushr system was enforced.
  • Took steps to eliminate the interest-based economy: bank accounts on profit and loss sharing, and investment in companies on the basis of partnership.
  • Education was based on Islamic teachings: Islamic Studies and Pakistan Studies were made compulsory up to graduation level, and Arabic was made a compulsory subject from class 6 to 8.

Afghan Jihad and its Impacts

In December 1979, the Soviet Army invaded Afghanistan, Pakistan's neighbouring Islamic country. Pakistan feared the Soviet Union would not stop there but would sweep through Pakistan to reach the sea and compete in trade with the USA, Europe and other rich countries. Pakistan opened its borders for the war-stricken Afghan refugees. President Zia called an emergency meeting of the foreign ministers of Muslim countries; they unanimously condemned the invasion and promised financial and moral support for the refugees.

  • Over three million Afghans took refuge in Pakistan.
  • The government could not confine the refugees to special camps; they spread over the entire country and established cottage colonies at many places.
  • Pakistan's economy suffered a lot from the influx, and the world community provided too little assistance for rehabilitation.
  • Concentration of refugees in urban areas created problems of health, hygiene and law and order.
  • Arms smuggling and narcotics caused instability in Pakistani society.

Key Points

  • Zia-ul-Haq imposed Martial Law on 5th July, 1977 after the PNA movement, and became President in August 1978.
  • Main Islamisation steps: Hadood Ordinance, Zakat and Ushr, prayer system, and the Shariah Ordinance (15th June, 1988).
  • Interest-free banking was promoted through profit and loss sharing accounts.
  • The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in December 1979 brought over three million Afghan refugees to Pakistan.
  • Refugees strained the economy and created health, law and order, arms smuggling and narcotics problems.

mcqs.why: After the PNA movement against alleged election rigging turned violent, the Chief of Army Staff General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq sacked Bhutto's government and imposed Martial Law on 5th July, 1977.

mcqs.q: When did Zia-ul-Haq designate himself President of Pakistan?
mcqs.why: Zia had promised elections in October 1977, but instead he formed his cabinet in August 1978 and designated himself President of Pakistan; he remained in power for more than eleven years.

mcqs.why: The Hadood Ordinance, the most important Islamisation step, enforced the four punishments clearly enshrined in the Holy Quran: for theft, adultery, wine drinking and false accusation of adultery.

mcqs.q: The Shariah Ordinance, declaring Islamic Shariah the supreme law of the country, was issued on:
mcqs.why: Zia issued the Shariah Ordinance on 15th June, 1988, declaring Islamic Shariah the supreme law of the country; earlier steps included the Hadood Ordinance and the Zakat and Ushr system.

mcqs.q: Who were appointed to establish and supervise the prayer system in offices under Zia's directives of 13th August 1984?
mcqs.why: On 13th August, 1984, Zia issued directives to establish the prayer system, and Prayer Monitors called Nazimeen-e-Salat were appointed; a prayer break during work hours had already been introduced in government offices.

mcqs.q: How did Zia's government try to eliminate the interest-based economy?
options: By introducing bank accounts on profit and loss sharing
mcqs.why: To eliminate interest, bank accounts were opened on profit and loss sharing and investment in companies was made on the basis of partnership, instead of the interest-based system.

mcqs.q: Up to which level were Islamic Studies and Pakistan Studies made compulsory under Zia's education policy?
mcqs.why: Education was based on Islamic teachings: Islamic Studies and Pakistan Studies were made compulsory up to graduation level, and Arabic was made a compulsory subject from class 6 to 8.

mcqs.q: When did the Soviet Army invade Afghanistan?
mcqs.why: In December 1979 the Soviet Army invaded Afghanistan, Pakistan's neighbouring Islamic country; Pakistan feared the Soviets would sweep through Pakistan to reach the sea.

mcqs.q: How many Afghan refugees took refuge in Pakistan after the Soviet invasion?
mcqs.why: Over three million Afghans took refuge in Pakistan; they could not be confined to special camps and spread over the entire country, straining the economy and creating health and law and order problems.

mcqs.q: Which problem did the Afghan refugees' presence create in Pakistani society?
mcqs.why: The notes list arms smuggling and narcotics among the harms of the refugee influx, along with pressure on the economy and problems of health, hygiene and law and order in urban areas.

lessons.title: Muhammad Khan Junejo's Government (1985-88)
lessons.notes_html:
After becoming President through referendum, Zia-ul-Haq announced general elections on a non-party basis. Elections for the National and Provincial Assemblies were held on 12th and 25th January, 1985 respectively. On 10th March, 1985, President Zia partially restored the Constitution of 1973 and, in consultation with the members of Parliament, nominated Muhammad Khan Junejo as Prime Minister. Junejo stated that democracy and martial law cannot go hand in hand, so martial law will be lifted soon — and he fulfilled his promise of lifting the martial law.

Five-Point Agenda of Junejo Government

  • Establishment of a strong Islamic democratic system, based on the Ideology of Pakistan.
  • Elimination of unemployment and establishment of an equitable economic system.
  • Elimination of illiteracy and laying the foundation of the country on a modern scientific basis.
  • Elimination of bribery and corruption, so as to dispense justice and provide security to people.
  • Safeguarding sovereignty and stability of the state with a balanced foreign policy.

8th Amendment and Dismissal

After the 1985 elections, during the Junejo Government, Parliament passed the 8th Amendment in the constitution. This Amendment delegated the powers of dismissal of a government and dissolution of Parliament to the President. In 1985, the Geneva Talks on the Afghan Issue entered a critical phase, over which President Zia-ul-Haq was not satisfied, and other differences also emerged between the two leaders. Ultimately, on 30th May, 1988, President Zia-ul-Haq dismissed the Junejo Government by exercising his power under the 8th Amendment.

On 17th August, 1988, while flying back from Bahawalpur to Islamabad, Zia-ul-Haq died in a plane crash. Ghulam Ishaq Khan (the then Chairman Senate) took oath as President and announced elections to be held in the next 90 days.

Key Points

  • Non-party elections were held on 12th and 25th January, 1985.
  • Muhammad Khan Junejo became Prime Minister on 10th March, 1985 and lifted martial law.
  • His five-point agenda covered Islamic democracy, unemployment, illiteracy, corruption and a balanced foreign policy.
  • The 8th Amendment gave the President power to dismiss a government and dissolve Parliament.
  • Zia dismissed the Junejo Government on 30th May, 1988 and died in a plane crash on 17th August, 1988.

mcqs.q: The non-party elections of 1985 for the National and Provincial Assemblies were held on:
mcqs.why: After becoming President through referendum, Zia announced non-party elections; they were held on 12th and 25th January, 1985 for the National and Provincial Assemblies respectively.

mcqs.q: When did Muhammad Khan Junejo become Prime Minister?
mcqs.why: On 10th March, 1985, President Zia partially restored the Constitution of 1973 and nominated Muhammad Khan Junejo as Prime Minister in consultation with the members of Parliament.

mcqs.q: What did Junejo say about democracy and martial law when he took office?
options: Both can continue together for five years
Democracy and martial law cannot go hand in hand
Elections should be held on party basis first
mcqs.why: Junejo stated that democracy and martial law cannot go hand in hand, so martial law would be lifted soon — and he fulfilled his promise of lifting the martial law.

mcqs.q: Which of the following was part of Junejo's Five-Point Agenda?
mcqs.why: Junejo's five-point agenda covered an Islamic democratic system, elimination of unemployment, elimination of illiteracy with a modern scientific basis, elimination of bribery and corruption, and safeguarding sovereignty with a balanced foreign policy.

mcqs.q: What power did the 8th Amendment give to the President?
options: Power to appoint the Chief Justice
Power to dismiss a government and dissolve Parliament
Power to appoint provincial governors only
mcqs.why: The 8th Amendment, passed during the Junejo Government, delegated to the President the powers of dismissal of a government and dissolution of Parliament.

mcqs.q: On which date did President Zia dismiss the Junejo Government?
mcqs.why: Differences emerged between Zia and Junejo, including over the Geneva Talks on Afghanistan; on 30th May, 1988, Zia dismissed the Junejo Government using his power under the 8th Amendment.

mcqs.q: How did Zia-ul-Haq die?
options: In a plane crash on 17th August, 1988
In a road accident near Bahawalpur
mcqs.why: On 17th August, 1988, while flying back from Bahawalpur to Islamabad, Zia-ul-Haq died in a plane crash; Ghulam Ishaq Khan, the Chairman Senate, then took oath as President.

mcqs.q: Who took oath as President after Zia's death?
mcqs.why: Ghulam Ishaq Khan, the then Chairman Senate, took oath as President after Zia's death and announced elections to be held within the next 90 days.

mcqs.q: The Geneva Talks of 1985, over which differences arose between Zia and Junejo, concerned which issue?
mcqs.why: In 1985 the Geneva Talks on the Afghan Issue entered a critical phase, over which President Zia-ul-Haq was not satisfied; other differences also emerged between the two leaders.

mcqs.q: Before nominating Junejo as Prime Minister, what did Zia partially restore on 10th March 1985?
mcqs.why: On 10th March, 1985, President Zia partially restored the Constitution of 1973 and, in consultation with the members of Parliament, nominated Muhammad Khan Junejo as Prime Minister.

lessons.title: Restoration of Democracy (1988-99)
lessons.notes_html:
President Ghulam Ishaq Khan held elections on 16th November, 1988. The Pakistan Peoples Party won 92 seats and Islami Jamhoori Ittehad (IJI) 54 seats in the National Assembly, so he invited Benazir Bhutto, leader of the majority party, to form the government.

Benazir Government: 1st Term (1988-90)

On 1st December, 1988, Benazir Bhutto took oath as Prime Minister. The IJI elected Mian Nawaz Sharif as Chief Minister of Punjab. Her steps were:

  • Political detainees were released and the ban on student organizations was lifted.
  • Newspapers and television were freed from government influence.
  • Thousands of jobless were employed under the Prime Minister's Employment Scheme.
  • Foreign exchange reserves, which had drastically reduced, were increased to triple.
  • The federal government started the Peoples Works Programme at country level.
  • International economic diplomacy succeeded: concessions in repayment terms of foreign loans and economic assistance of over 3 billion US dollars.
  • The fourth SAARC Summit was held at Islamabad, and the Pakistan-India treaty of not attacking each other's nuclear installations was signed.

Benazir considered the 8th Amendment a threat and consulted the opposition to annul it, but the opposition wanted all amendments in the 1973 Constitution abolished, which she did not accept, so it could not be annulled. Her relations with Chief Minister Nawaz Sharif in Punjab were not friendly, causing political instability. On 6th August, 1990, President Ghulam Ishaq Khan dissolved the assemblies under the 8th Amendment and declared a State of Emergency.

Nawaz Sharif Government: 1st Term (1990-93)

Fresh elections were held on 24th October, 1990. The IJI won 105 out of 206 seats while the Peoples Democratic Alliance got 45. On 6th November, 1990, Nawaz Sharif was elected Prime Minister.

  • He launched the "Self Employment Scheme" to reduce unemployment — youths were given loans of fifty thousand to three lacs rupees per head to set up their own business.
  • He launched a development plan called "Tameer-e-Watan Programme".
  • On 22nd January, 1991, he set up the Privatisation Commission to bring reforms in the banking and corporate sectors.
  • Through the National Finance Commission Award (NFC Award), his government allayed the grievances of the small provinces about division of fiscal resources.
  • For agriculture: taxes on imports of agricultural equipment were reduced, support prices of rice, cotton and sugarcane were increased, and taxes on cotton exports were reduced.
  • On 20th December, 1992, a Ten-year Educational Plan was announced: admission to 100% children in schools till 2002, raising the literacy rate from 34% to 70%; four universities in the public sector and twelve in the private sector; vocational training at middle school level for technical education.

On 18th April, 1993, President Ghulam Ishaq Khan dissolved the Nawaz Government. Speaker Gohar Ayub Khan challenged this in the Supreme Court, which restored the government on 26th May, 1993. Differences between Nawaz Sharif and the President became so severe that the Army had to intervene, and both of them had to resign.

Benazir Government: 2nd Term (1993-96)

In the 1993 elections, the PPP won 86 seats, Muslim League (Nawaz group) 72 seats and Muslim League (Junejo group) 7 seats. The PPP formed a coalition government with the Junejo group; Benazir Bhutto became Prime Minister again and the Chief Ministership of Punjab was given to the Muslim League (Junejo Group).

  • She stopped all development projects of Nawaz's regime and launched new ones — the Lahore By-Pass road and the Karachi Flyover are worth mentioning.
  • Loan procedure was made easy for farmers and the Awami Tractor Scheme was launched to provide them tractors.
  • Separate police stations for women were established.
  • Relations with India remained tense; she rejected international pressure to roll back Pakistan's nuclear programme and made an arms supply agreement with France.

The country faced critical political crises: the MQM was a tough challenge in Sindh, and in Punjab the tussle over Chief Minister Manzoor Wattoo — blamed for distributing development funds only among his party affiliates — followed by Sardar Arif Nakai's appointment, the court's reinstatement of Wattoo, and his dissolution of the Punjab Assembly created further instability. Due to this tussle and other allegations, President Farooq Ahmed Khan Laghari dismissed the Benazir Government under the 8th Amendment.

Nawaz Sharif Government: 2nd Term (1997-99)

In the 1997 elections, Muslim League (Nawaz Group) won 137 seats — more than a two-third majority. Shahbaz Sharif became Chief Minister of Punjab; in Sindh, the Nawaz League allied with MQM and appointed Liaquat Jatoi as Chief Minister. With the required two-third majority, Nawaz Sharif annulled the 8th Amendment by adopting the 13th Amendment.

  • Despite strong international pressure, he allowed Pakistani scientists to conduct nuclear test explosions on 28th May, 1998.
  • The Islamabad-Lahore Motorway was completed.
  • "Khidmat Committees" were formed to address public issues at local level, but this step could not serve any purpose.
  • Ordinances like Qisas and Diyat laws (talion laws), anti-narcotics and accountability laws were passed.
  • In February 1998, he announced the 2010 programme: loans for house building, police reforms, and holding competitive examinations in Urdu language.

Key Points

  • Democracy was restored with the elections of 16th November, 1988; Benazir Bhutto became Prime Minister on 1st December, 1988.
  • Benazir's first government was dismissed on 6th August, 1990 under the 8th Amendment.
  • Nawaz Sharif's first term brought the Self Employment Scheme, Tameer-e-Watan Programme, Privatisation Commission and the NFC Award.
  • Benazir's second government (1993-96) was also dismissed by President Farooq Laghari under the 8th Amendment.
  • Nawaz Sharif's second term annulled the 8th Amendment through the 13th Amendment and completed the Islamabad-Lahore Motorway.
  • No government in 1988-99 completed its term; the 8th Amendment was the main cause of dismissals.

mcqs.why: The PPP won 92 seats and the Islami Jamhoori Ittehad (IJI) 54 seats, so President Ghulam Ishaq Khan invited Benazir Bhutto, leader of the majority party, to form the government.

mcqs.why: Benazir Bhutto took oath as Prime Minister on 1st December, 1988; the IJI elected Mian Nawaz Sharif as Chief Minister of Punjab in the same period.

mcqs.q: The fourth SAARC Summit during Benazir's first term was held at:
mcqs.why: The fourth SAARC Summit was held at Islamabad, and the Pakistan-India treaty of not attacking each other's nuclear installations was also signed during her first term.

mcqs.q: When was Benazir's first government dismissed?
mcqs.why: On 6th August, 1990, President Ghulam Ishaq Khan dissolved the assemblies under the 8th Amendment and declared a State of Emergency, ending Benazir's first government.

mcqs.q: Under Nawaz Sharif's Self Employment Scheme, youths were given loans of:
options: Ten thousand to one lac rupees per head

mcqs.why: The Self Employment Scheme gave youths loans of fifty thousand to three lacs rupees per head to set up their own business and reduce unemployment.

mcqs.q: When did Nawaz Sharif set up the Privatisation Commission?
mcqs.why: On 22nd January, 1991, Nawaz Sharif set up the Privatisation Commission to bring reforms in the banking and corporate sectors; he also launched the Tameer-e-Watan Programme.

mcqs.q: The Ten-year Educational Plan of 20th December 1992 aimed to raise the literacy rate from 34% to:
mcqs.why: The plan aimed at admission of 100% children in schools till 2002 and raising the literacy rate from 34% to 70%; the required rise is 70 - 34 = 36 percentage points.

mcqs.q: What happened after President Ghulam Ishaq Khan dissolved the Nawaz Government on 18th April 1993?
options: The Supreme Court restored the government on 26th May, 1993
Fresh elections were held at once
mcqs.why: Speaker Gohar Ayub Khan challenged the dissolution in the Supreme Court, which restored the government on 26th May, 1993; later, differences became so severe that both Nawaz Sharif and the President had to resign.

mcqs.q: Through which amendment did Nawaz Sharif annul the 8th Amendment in his second term?
mcqs.why: With a two-third majority in 1997, Nawaz Sharif annulled the 8th Amendment by adopting the 13th Amendment; his government also completed the Islamabad-Lahore Motorway.

lessons.title: Nuclear Tests
lessons.notes_html:
Since the partition of the Subcontinent, relations between Pakistan and India have never been cordial. In 1998, an extremist Hindu political party, the "Bharatia Janta Party", came into power in India. It started threatening Pakistan, declared its goal to capture the remaining part of Kashmir (Azad Kashmir) also from Pakistan, and announced to build the Ram Temple on the site of the Babri Mosque. At the same time, India was improving her nuclear technology.

India's Nuclear Tests

In early May, 1998, India conducted nuclear test explosions in Rajasthan. Proud of this success, the Indian government and its media started threatening Pakistan. India's Interior Minister, L.K. Adwani, warned Pakistan that if she did not stop interfering in Kashmir, India would have all rights to attack her. India also demanded from the international community to make her a permanent member of the Security Council and give her the Veto Power.

Pakistan's Response

The world knew Pakistan had nuclear capability, though she had not declared it. The USA, Britain and other Western countries pressurised Pakistan not to test its nuclear capability, but the opposition parties and the people insisted Pakistan must show its nuclear capability to deter India from aggression. At this critical juncture, Pakistan rejected the international pressure and conducted six nuclear test explosions in the Chaghi Hills on 28th May, 1998. Thus, Pakistan became the first Nuclear Power in the Muslim World.

Effects of the Tests

  • A State of Emergency was declared immediately in the country to stop the drain of capital abroad.
  • Some Western countries individually imposed sanctions on Pakistan.
  • The Sanction Resolution of the UN Security Council was vetoed by Pakistan's friendly country, China.

Events After the Tests

In the early days of his 2nd term, Nawaz Sharif picked up differences with the then Chief Justice of Pakistan, Syed Sajjad Ali Shah. After a few months of tussle, the Chief Justice resigned; President Farooq Ahmad Khan Laghari, who liked the stance of the Chief Justice, also resigned. Muhammad Rafiq Tarar was appointed the new President. Later, the government wanted changes in the army ranks too. On 12th October, 1999, the government ordered the dismissal of the then Chief of Army Staff, General Pervez Musharraf, who was on a foreign trip, and the ceremony of handing over charge to Lt. General Zia-ud-Din was about to start when the acting supreme command of the army launched a coup against Nawaz Sharif and arrested him. When General Musharraf landed in the country, he took over the government, suspended the constitution and declared himself the Chief Executive of Pakistan.

Key Points

  • India conducted nuclear tests in Rajasthan in early May 1998 and threatened Pakistan.
  • Western countries pressurised Pakistan not to test, but the people and opposition demanded a reply.
  • Pakistan conducted six nuclear tests in the Chaghi Hills on 28th May, 1998.
  • Pakistan became the first nuclear power in the Muslim World.
  • Emergency was declared and some Western countries imposed sanctions; China vetoed the UN Security Council sanction resolution.

lessons.title: Pervez Musharraf's Government (1999-2008)
lessons.notes_html:
After taking over the government on 12th October, 1999, General Pervez Musharraf announced a 7-point agenda, which included ending political and other sorts of corruption, strengthening the economy and devolution of powers down to the grass-root level. He decided to introduce the system of Local Self-Government.

Devolution of Power and Local Self-Government

On 14th August, 2000, Pervez Musharraf announced the System of Local Self-Governments, aimed at empowering the people at local level and bringing genuine democracy to the country. Local Government is a democratic body which resolves local issues by using its authority and resources, allows people to make decisions on their local problems and supervise the administration. Under the Devolution Plan, powers were transferred to the Union Council, Tehsil Council and District Government. For Local Bodies elections, the minimum age limit for a voter was 18 years and elections were conducted on a non-party basis. By July 2001 the elections were completed, and on 14th August, 2001 the elected bodies started functioning.

Organizational Structure of Local Government, 2001

The Local Self-Governments Ordinance, 2001 contained these tiers:

  • Union Council: The foundation level. Every Union Council comprised 21 members, including reserved seats for women and minorities. It was headed by the "Union Nazim"; in his absence the Deputy Nazim acted for him, and the Union Secretary served under the Nazim. Its functions were to approve annual development plans and look after roads, streets and sewerage; a justice committee in each Union Council mediated in local disputes.
  • Tehsil Council: It comprised the Deputy Nazims of all Union Councils in the Tehsil; 33% seats were reserved for women and 5% each for labourers, farmers and minorities. The Tehsil Nazim was head of the Tehsil, and the Town Municipal Officer coordinated the departments. Its functions included urban and rural planning, development plans, water supply and sewerage, health, hygiene and sanitation, and construction of roads.
  • District Government: It comprised the District Nazim, Deputy Nazim, District Council and district administration. The District Nazim was head of the district administration and in-charge of all district level departments, including police. The Provincial Government deputed a District Coordination Officer (DCO) in every district to coordinate all government departments, and every district level department was headed by an Executive District Officer (EDO). Its mandate included approval of the annual monetary budget, framing development plans, and sanitary and construction works in urban areas.
  • City Governments: Formed in big cities like Karachi, Lahore, Peshawar, Faisalabad, Multan, Hyderabad and Quetta, to look after public transport, intra-city roads, sanitation and development plans.

General Elections, 2002

Musharraf fulfilled his promise of elections in 2002. Elections for the National and Provincial Assemblies were held simultaneously. People elected 272 members of the National Assembly; in addition there were 60 reserved seats for women and 10 for minorities. These elections were unique: many senior politicians could not take part because they could not meet the criterion of having a graduation degree, and for the first time the distinction of Muslim and non-Muslim for general seats was eliminated — the Joint Electorate System was adopted, so minorities could also contest any general seat and vote for Muslim and non-Muslim candidates.

  • Muttahida Majlas-e-Amal (MMA) — an alliance of religious parties — won 51 seats.
  • Muslim League (Quaid-e-Azam Group) won 76 seats; Pakistan Peoples Party 62 seats; Muslim League (Nawaz Group) 14 seats.
  • No single party had enough majority; 10 PPP members, called the Forward Block, joined Muslim League (Quaid-e-Azam Group).
  • Mir Zafarullah Jamali of Muslim League (Quaid-e-Azam Group) was elected Prime Minister, with the support of MMA.
  • In Balochistan, Muslim League (Quaid-e-Azam Group) formed a coalition government with MMA; in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, MMA formed its exclusive government; in Punjab and Sindh, Muslim League (Quaid-e-Azam Group) was invited to form the government.

Enlightened Moderation

General Pervez Musharraf often used the phrase enlightened moderation. He meant a way of life based on scientific knowledge and artistic creation, interfaith tolerance, freedom of knowledge and freedom of speech, on the condition of regarding the basic virtue of humanity and the traditional social norms.

Industrial Growth and Privatization

During previous governments the economy had declined: public sector performance was poor, fiscal strength was weak, and almost all public sector banks, railway, PIA, Karachi Steel Mills and WAPDA were running in deficit. Musharraf stabilised the economy and took measures for the growth of industry. To assure foreign investors of the safety of their capital, he adopted the policy of privatization — public sector enterprises running in loss were sold to the private sector. As a result, the economy started growing at an annual rate of 6% and foreign exchange reserves rose to 12.5 billion US dollars.

Economic Reforms

In the initial days of Musharraf's rule the national economy was weak and foreign and domestic debt had increased manifold; due to the bad law and order situation, foreign investors had lost faith. Musharraf encouraged them so that employment opportunities could be created and the economy stabilised. Besides other poverty alleviation programmes, he granted loans to people, especially the youth, to establish their own business. In the last few years of his government, the country's annual economic growth rate increased to 7%.

Key Points

  • Musharraf took over on 12th October, 1999 as Chief Executive and announced a 7-point agenda.
  • The Local Self-Government system was announced on 14th August, 2000; elected bodies started working on 14th August, 2001.
  • The 2001 system had Union Council, Tehsil Council, District Government and City Governments.
  • The 2002 elections introduced the graduation condition and the Joint Electorate System; Mir Zafarullah Jamali became Prime Minister.
  • Enlightened moderation meant a way of life based on scientific knowledge, artistic creation and interfaith tolerance.
  • Privatization of loss-making enterprises raised growth to 6% and reserves to 12.5 billion US dollars; growth later reached 7%.

mcqs.why: Mir Zafarullah Jamali of Muslim League (Quaid-e-Azam Group), which won 76 seats, was elected Prime Minister with the support of MMA, which had won 51 seats.

lessons.title: Geo-Political Importance
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan holds immense political importance because of its geo-strategic position. Its location makes it important for the Gulf States, for China, for Russia and for the whole Muslim World.

Pakistan and the Gulf States

The Gulf States, which are rich in oil reserves, lie to the west of Pakistan. Most of the energy requirements of the industrially developed world are met by these countries. In return, different goods are exported to the Gulf States. Pakistan's sea ports are quite useful for transit routes.

Pakistan, China and America

Pakistan shares its border with China, which is rapidly emerging as a first class world power. America and some other powerful countries are rivals to China's international role. In this perspective, Pakistan holds great importance for both countries.

Pakistan and Russia

Russia is also a world power. Although Pakistan does not share a border with her, she cannot ignore Pakistan's geo-strategic position. In the past, Russia, as the Soviet Union, had expansionist designs of getting access to Pakistan's coastline so that she could control the world's sea-trade routes. That is why when in 1979 Soviet forces occupied Afghanistan, the West fully supported Pakistan and the Afghans against the Soviet invasion.

Centre of the Muslim World

Pakistan is located in the centre of the Muslim World:

  • To the east and south-east there lives a huge Muslim minority in India, and there lie the Islamic countries of Bangladesh, Maldives, Malaysia, Indonesia and Brunei.
  • To the north and north-west, from Afghanistan to Siberia and the Caucasus Mountains, lies a vast stretch of land of the believers in the oneness of Allah.
  • To the west and south-west, from Turkey up to the Atlantic Ocean, the Islamic World is stretched over.

Pakistan has the privilege of being the first Nuclear Power of the Muslim World.

Key Points

  • Pakistan's importance comes from its geo-strategic position.
  • The oil-rich Gulf States lie to its west; its sea ports serve as transit routes.
  • It borders China, a rising first class world power and a rival of America.
  • Russia wanted access to Pakistan's coastline to control world sea-trade routes.
  • In 1979 the West supported Pakistan and the Afghans against the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan.
  • Pakistan sits in the centre of the Muslim World and is its first Nuclear Power.

lessons.title: Objectives of Pakistan's Foreign Policy
lessons.notes_html:
The modern means of transportation and communication have turned the world into a global village. All countries must maintain mutual relations for their needs in defence, economic and social sectors. The policy which a country formulates to develop relations with other countries is called its foreign policy. As the main objective in the creation of Pakistan was to safeguard and promote Islamic ideology, this principle holds a central position in our foreign policy.

i. Preservation of Regional Integrity and Freedom

Since independence, some countries have been conspiring against Pakistan to weaken its administrative capability and sovereignty. So the preservation of national integrity and freedom is the key objective. Pakistan also extends moral and diplomatic support to nations deprived of their freedom, such as Kashmir and Palestine. Pakistan pursues a non-interference policy and does not allow any other country to interfere in her internal affairs.

ii. Protection of Ideological Basis

Islam is the foundation of Pakistan Ideology. Safeguarding this basis is an important objective, achieved by promoting relations with countries which believe in the same ideology. So establishing friendly relations with the Muslim countries is the main objective of Pakistan's foreign policy. Allama Iqbal gave guidelines for this in his verse, whose sense is that the profit and loss of the whole community is one, and the Prophet, the religion and the Quran of all are one.

iii. Economic Development

The prosperity of the people and the stability of a country are linked with economic development. Pakistan wishes to develop relations with countries with which she can establish bilateral trade. Pakistan tries to persuade the rich countries of the world to make investments in the country. This raises government income in the form of taxes and also creates job opportunities.

iv. Promotion of Culture

Architecture, sports, dress, customs, traditions, moral values and religious beliefs form the culture of a nation, and religion has a great impact on culture. Pakistanis are known for their Islamic ideology and distinct culture. Governments have made serious efforts to develop cultural ties with all nations. One objective of establishing the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) was to strengthen cultural ties among member states; easy visas are issued so people can travel easily within the region.

Key Points

  • Foreign policy is the policy for developing relations with other countries.
  • Islamic ideology holds the central position in Pakistan's foreign policy.
  • First objective: preservation of national integrity and freedom, with non-interference.
  • Pakistan supports deprived nations such as Kashmir and Palestine.
  • Protection of the ideological basis means close friendly relations with Muslim countries.
  • Economic development is sought through bilateral trade and foreign investment.
  • Promotion of culture includes cultural ties through bodies like SAARC.

lessons.title: Relations with Neighboring Countries
lessons.notes_html:
Peaceful co-existence is the main objective of Pakistan's foreign policy. Pakistan has always tried to let the people of this region live in peace and use their resources for raising their living standard.

i. Relations with India

Relations between Pakistan and India have always been tense. In the early days India blocked the canal water, created hurdles in the division of assets and persecuted the Muslim minority. On 8th April, 1950, an agreement was signed between Prime Minister Liaqat Ali Khan and Indian Prime Minister Jawahar Lal Nehru to protect the rights of minorities in both countries. In 1948 India occupied a large area of Kashmir by military invasion (see the Kashmir Issue lesson). In 1960, due to President Ayub Khan's compromising policy, the Indus Basin Treaty was signed: India got the waters of Ravi, Sutlaj and Beas, while Pakistan got the waters of Indus, Jhelum and Chenab. India has since been violating it by constructing dams on Pakistani rivers. In 1965 India thrust a war on Pakistan, and in 1971 she played an important role in the separation of East Pakistan. In 1974 India conducted nuclear test explosions, and since 1984 she has been trying to get control over Siachin Glacier. In 1990, during Mian Nawaz Sharif's government, relations started improving: the Friendship Bus Service was started and bilateral trade relations were established, but these could not last long. In May 1998 India again conducted nuclear tests; in response Pakistan also conducted six nuclear tests, which balanced the military power in the region. In 2001 President Pervez Musharraf met Indian Prime Minister Wajpai in Agra, but Wajpai's ministers and advisors created hurdles in signing the agreement, so the President returned in despair.

ii. Relations with China

Pakistan was the first Islamic state which recognized China, and it supported China in attaining membership of the UNO. When war broke out between China and Korea, Pakistan refused to vote for trade sanctions against China, refused to send troops to Korea on UNO's demand, and declared the Tibet issue an internal matter of China. Joining the South-East Asian Treaty Organization (SEATO) meant direct opposition of China, yet Pakistan continued moral and diplomatic support for her. In return, China fully supported Pakistan in the 1965 war by deploying troops to the Indian borders, and after the war she enhanced Pakistan's military aid. The Ordnance Factory, Wah and the Heavy Mechanical Complex, Taxila are proof of this friendship. China played a key role in the construction of the Karakuram Highway, and her assistance in the Chashma Nuclear Power Plant, the Coastal Highway in Balochistan and Gwadar Port further strengthened it. Pakistan has assembled J.F.17 Thunder fighter jets in collaboration with China, considered equally capable as the American F-16. In 1998, when many countries wanted a trade embargo on Pakistan, China vetoed the resolution in the UN Security Council. China's international trade has increased by 29.5% and her exchange reserves have grown up to one trillion US dollars. The Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and the Gwadar-Kashghar Economic Corridor are testimonies of her drive for defence and economic relations.

iii. Relations with Afghanistan

Pakistan and Afghanistan are Muslim countries sharing historic, cultural and religious values, yet their relations have never been friendly. In 1947 Afghanistan was the only country that voted against Pakistan's membership in the UNO, and she does not recognize the Durand Line as the international border. Despite this, Pakistan established diplomatic relations with her in 1948 and provided trade facilities. During 1956-58 relations improved: air, telegraph and telephone services started and transit trade agreements were made. In 1958 relations suffered again and diplomatic contacts were suspended; in 1963, by the mediation of the Shah of Iran, relations were restored. In the wars of 1965 and 1971 the Afghan government remained neutral but the Afghan people fully supported Pakistan. Sardar Daud's rule lasted till April 1978; the Peoples Democratic Party led by Noor Muhammad Tarakai removed him on 27th April, 1978 — the Saur Revolution. Under the Afghan-Soviet Pact of 1978, Soviet military intruded into Afghanistan on 12th December, 1979, and about three million Afghans took refuge in Pakistan. Under the Geneva Accord the Soviet Army withdrew in 1989, yet civil war continued. In September 1996 the Taliban Movement established its rule, and on 24th May, 1997 Pakistan formally recognized the Taliban Government. After the attack on the World Trade Centre on 11th September, 2001, American military invaded Afghanistan on October 17, 2001 and abolished the Taliban regime; in 2003 a joint army of 43 other countries of NATO also entered Afghanistan. On December 22, 2001 a transitional government was set up under Hamid Karzai. In January 2002 Pakistan reopened her embassy and announced 100 million US dollars for reconstruction. Karzai became President in 2004 and again in 2009; a Pak-Afghan transit trade agreement was signed in 2011. After the June 2014 elections, Ashraf Ghani became President and Abdullah Abdullah Chief-Executive — a new era of Pak-Afghan friendship.

iv. Relations with Iran

Iran was the first country to recognize Pakistan after independence. She helped Pakistan in the rehabilitation of refugees, and the Shah of Iran's efforts brought Pakistan and Afghanistan to friendly terms. In July 1964 Pakistan, Iran and Turkey signed the Regional Cooperation for Development (RCD), renamed in January 1985 as the Economic Cooperation Organization (ECO); later Afghanistan and the six Muslim states of Central Asia were also admitted. Iran has consistently supported Pakistan's position on the Kashmir issue, supported Pakistan in the wars of 1965 and 1971 and supported the May 1998 nuclear tests. Pakistan has extended full diplomatic support to the Iranian nuclear programme. A Gas Pipeline Project between the two countries is under process.

v. Relations with SAARC Countries

In the late 1970s the President of Bangladesh, Zia-ur-Rahman, proposed an economic block of South Asian states. This was materialized in December 1985 as the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC). Its founding members were Pakistan, India, Bangladesh, Sri Lanka, Maldives, Bhutan and Nepal; in April 2007, at the 14th SAARC summit, Afghanistan was admitted as the 8th member. At the foreign secretaries' meeting at Colombo in August 1981, the fields listed for mutual cooperation were: (1) Agriculture, (2) Rural Development, (3) Environment, (4) Health and Population, (5) Communication. Pakistan takes steps such as exchange of cultural delegations, educational scholarships, economic cooperation, poverty reduction and cooperation in science and technology.

Key Points

  • With India: Liaqat-Nehru agreement 8 April 1950; Indus Basin Treaty 1960; wars in 1965 and 1971; both tested nuclear weapons in May 1998; Agra meeting 2001 failed.
  • China is a tested friend: support in 1965, Karakuram Highway, Gwadar Port, J.F.17 Thunder and a veto for Pakistan in 1998.
  • Afghanistan voted against Pakistan in the UNO in 1947 and disputes the Durand Line, yet Pakistan sheltered about three million Afghan refugees.
  • Iran was the first country to recognize Pakistan; RCD (1964) later became ECO (1985).
  • SAARC was formed in December 1985 with seven founding members; Afghanistan joined as 8th member in April 2007.

lessons.title: Relations with Muslim World
lessons.notes_html:
Promoting relations with the Muslim countries is the primary objective of Pakistan's foreign policy. Pakistan is an active and influential member of the Organisation of Islamic Countries (OIC).

The OIC

The OIC was founded in 1969 at Rabat, a city of Morocco. In August 1969 Israel set the Al Aqsa Mosque (Baitul Muqaddas) on fire; this tragic incident motivated the Muslim World to create a forum to unitedly confront the dangers posed to them. Pakistan was a member of the committee in charge of organising the conference. The most important meeting of the OIC is the summit conference, held after every three years; the conference of foreign ministers is held at least once a year. The OIC has sub-organisations like the Islamic Development Bank, Islamic Unity Fund and Al Quds Fund. Its objectives include protecting the rights of Palestinians, eradicating poverty and illiteracy from the Muslim World and promoting cooperation.

i. (a) Relations with Saudi Arabia

Pakistan is deeply affiliated to Saudi Arabia by religious, cultural and trade relations. The land of Saudi Arabia is held in high esteem because each year millions of Muslims visit it to perform Hajj. Saudi Arabia recognized Pakistan immediately after independence; in 1954 the people of Pakistan warmly welcomed Saudi King Saud bin Abdul Aziz. Saudi Arabia extended moral and financial support in every critical situation and overtly assisted Pakistan in the wars of 1965 and 1971; King Faisal took personal interest in the Islamic Summit Conference held in Pakistan in February 1974. In 1974 Saudi Arabia granted an interest-free loan of one billion dollars for construction and expansion in cement and fertilizer industries. Under the Pak-Saudi pact of February 1984, Pakistan sent 4,000 military experts to train the Saudi Armed Forces. Pakistan exports manpower, rice, cotton textile, tents and handicrafts to Saudi Arabia; Saudi Arabia provides Pakistan with petroleum at low price.

i. (b) Relations with Other Arab Countries

The Arab world includes Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Jordon, Syria, Lebanon, Kuwait, United Arab Emirates, Yemen, Egypt, Libya, Tunis, Sudan and Morocco. A large number of Pakistanis work in these oil-rich states and their remittances greatly support Pakistan's economy. The United Arab Emirates has been providing financial aid which enabled Pakistan to complete many projects. Pakistan played a vital role in ending the civil war in Lebanon and strongly condemned Israel's invasion of Lebanon in 1982; Pakistan has always condemned Israeli aggression in Palestine at all diplomatic forums. Libya gave Pakistan full diplomatic support plus military and economic aid in the 1971 war. During the Egypt-Israel War of 1973, Pakistan extended full diplomatic and military support to Egypt and played a key role in admitting Egypt to the OIC.

ii. Relations with Turkey

Pakistan and Turkey are friends on the basis of historic, cultural and religious commonalities. They shared the Central Treaty Organization (CENTO) and are now partners in the ECO. Turkey has always supported the right of self-determination of the Kashmiri people and gave Pakistan financial and moral support in the wars of 1965 and 1971. On the Cyprus issue, Pakistan strongly favoured Turkey's stance at every international forum. The two help each other in commerce and industry, have strategic military ties, and Turkey has recently helped Pakistan improve her F-16 fighter planes.

iii. Relations with Central Asian States

The disintegration of the Soviet Union in 1991 liberated the Central Asian Muslim states: Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kirghizstan and Azerbaijan. Pakistan established cultural and trade relations with them and helped them become members of the ECO. These states are rich in mineral resources but are land-locked, so Pakistan assists them by providing transit facilities through Karachi port; Gwadar port is another option for their trade needs. High rank military and civil officials frequently exchange visits.

Key Points

  • OIC was founded in 1969 at Rabat after Israel set the Al Aqsa Mosque on fire in August 1969.
  • Saudi Arabia gave an interest-free loan of one billion dollars in 1974 and petroleum at low price; Pakistan sent 4,000 military experts in 1984.
  • Pakistanis working in Arab states send remittances that support Pakistan's economy.
  • Pakistan supported Egypt in 1973, condemned Israel's 1982 invasion of Lebanon, and backs Palestine everywhere.
  • Turkey supports Kashmiri self-determination; Pakistan supports Turkey on the Cyprus issue.
  • Land-locked Central Asian states, free since 1991, use Karachi and Gwadar ports for trade.

lessons.title: Kashmir Issue
lessons.notes_html:
The Jammu and Kashmir region lies to the north-east of Pakistan. It is the most sensitive issue between Pakistan and India, and Pakistan has always tried to resolve it peacefully.

How the Issue Began

According to the 3rd June, 1947 Plan of partition of India, autonomous states were given the choice of accession, either to Pakistan or India, by considering the wishes of the people of these states. The Muslim population in the state of Jammu and Kashmir was 77%, but the ruler of Kashmir at that time was a Hindu Raja. The Dogra Raja started using delay tactics in deciding the accession of the Kashmir state.

Massacre and Armed Struggle

  • Kashmiri Hindus committed the massacre of Kashmiri Muslims with the support of India, to force them to migrate to Pakistan.
  • Many retired Muslim soldiers of the British Army were at Poonch. They started an armed struggle under the leadership of Sardar Abdul Qayum Khan.
  • The Kashmiri Raja fled to India, took refuge there and declared the accession of Kashmir state to India.
  • On the pretext of supporting the Raja for restoration of peace, Indian forces entered Kashmir.
  • Pakistan was not militarily strong enough, but tribesmen of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa voluntarily joined the Kashmir freedom movement.
  • India raised hue and cry in the UN Security Council, accusing Pakistan of invading Kashmir.

UNO Resolutions

The Security Council set up a commission, which submitted its report on 6th February, 1948, stating to hold a plebiscite in Kashmir. Another resolution was passed on 5th January, 1949, declaring plebiscite as the only solution to this issue. The Security Council decided to nominate a military observer and devised a procedure for conducting the plebiscite. According to the UN Security Council resolutions, the issue should be resolved by giving the right of self-determination to Kashmiris; India deprives Kashmiris of this right because she knows that if a plebiscite is held, the Muslim majority of Kashmir would decide to join Pakistan, so she ignores the United Nations' resolutions.

Present Position

India started evading the Security Council's resolutions and tried to suppress the freedom movement, but the movement got more momentum. Thousands of Kashmiris have been martyred, women and children are harassed daily and houses are set on fire. Pakistan has always stressed the peaceful resolution of the Kashmir issue in accordance with the wishes of the Kashmiri people and has held table talks with India, but Indian leaders create hurdles by declaring Kashmir an integral part of India.

Key Points

  • Under the 3rd June 1947 Plan, states were to join Pakistan or India according to the wishes of their people.
  • Kashmir's population was 77% Muslim, but its ruler was a Hindu Dogra Raja who delayed accession.
  • After the massacre of Muslims, Poonch soldiers rose under Sardar Abdul Qayum Khan; the Raja fled and declared accession to India.
  • UN commission report of 6 February 1948 and resolution of 5 January 1949 made plebiscite the only solution.
  • India evades the UN resolutions and calls Kashmir its integral part.
  • Pakistan wants a peaceful solution according to the wishes of the Kashmiri people.

lessons.title: Pakistan and the Super Powers of the World
lessons.notes_html:
This lesson covers Pakistan's relations with the world powers: America, Russia, Japan and the European countries.

i. Relations with America

On 23rd September, 1947, the USA appointed her ambassador to Pakistan. In early 1949 the Soviet Union invited Prime Minister Liaqat Ali Khan to visit Moscow, but he preferred the invitation from the USA; during his visit, Quaid-e-Millat addressed the US Congress. In 1953 the USA helped Pakistan overcome the food crisis. With US help, SEATO came into being in 1954 and the Central Treaty Organization (CENTO) was formed in February 1955, involving Pakistan, Iran and Turkey; through both pacts Pakistan obtained a large supply of arms. In 1959 US President Eisenhower visited Pakistan and promised continued military aid and financial support for the second five-year plan. In 1964 the USA declared that she did not recognize India-held Kashmir as a legitimate part of India. Yet during the September 1965 war the USA did nothing for Pakistan and blamed her for the war, so Pakistan reconsidered her foreign policy and in 1968 shut down the US air station near Peshawar. In 1971 too the USA ignored Pakistan's interests and suspended aid. In February 1975 Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto visited the USA and the ban on arms supply was lifted. In March 1976 Pakistan started her peaceful atomic programme, which the USA opposed bitterly. After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, the USA announced three million dollars as economic and military aid, and on 22nd November, 1982 sanctioned the sale of forty F-16 fighter planes. After the Soviet withdrawal, the USA pressurised Pakistan to back away from nuclear capability, but Pakistan did not compromise; when Pakistan answered the Indian nuclear explosion with its own tests, the US and many European countries suspended aid. After 11th September, 2001, the USA needed Pakistan's assistance against global terrorism and immediately offered one billion dollars as economic and military aid; presently the USA appreciates Pakistan's efforts and continues aid.

ii. Relations with Russia

Diplomatic relations between Pakistan and Russia were established in 1948. In 1949 Russia (then the USSR) invited Liaqat Ali Khan, but he preferred to visit the USA, so Russia considered Pakistan a US ally and started favouring India; after Pakistan joined SEATO and CENTO, Russia began vetoing UN resolutions on Kashmir in India's favour. Still, in 1958 Russia showed interest in establishing a steel mill in Pakistan. During President Ayub's era an agreement was signed for exploration of petroleum, air service resumed, and cooperation started in education, literature, arts and science. In the 1965 war Russia played an imminent role in reconciliation, and Pakistan and India signed the Tashkend Declaration. On 30th May, 1965, the Russian prime minister paid a one-day visit to Pakistan, ending in a joint communique on cooperation. In 1971 Russia openly supported India and vetoed the UN resolution to declare India the aggressor. Prime Minister Zulfiqar Ali Bhutto then visited Russia and normalized relations; Russia offered enough aid to establish and expand the Pakistan Steel Mills, Karachi. Relations became tense again with the 1979 invasion of Afghanistan. In December 1991, after the withdrawal of the Russian Army from Afghanistan, the Soviet Union disintegrated; a new era of Pak-Russia relations started — Russia now appreciates Pakistan's efforts against terrorism and emphasises that Pakistan and India should resolve their issues, including Kashmir, through bilateral dialogues.

iii. Relations with Japan

Japan is an economic giant. Diplomatic relations were established in 1952, and in 1957 the prime ministers of both countries exchanged visits. Pakistan imports parts of heavy industry, electrical appliances, transport machinery and chemical goods from Japan, and exports raw cotton and fish to her; Japan has also been providing loans. In 1960 Japan provided assistance in the industrial development of Pakistan. Her Balochistan projects include the Diesel Power Station Project in Pasni, 1988, the Guddu-Sibi-Quetta Power Transmission Project, supply of educational/scientific equipment to Balochistan Engineering College, Khuzdar, 1988, and the project of exploring groundwater resources in Balochistan. The first agreement on exchange of cultural delegations was signed in 1957, and in 1973 Japan provided financial aid for the preservation of the archaeological site of Mohenjo Daro.

iv. Relations with European Countries

Pakistan has extensive trade relations with European countries, which assist her in agriculture, industries, defence and education. In March 1976 relations with France lost warmth when she refused to provide an atomic reactor for the Chashma Nuclear Power Plant; later, in 1979, France signed an agreement to provide Mirage fighter jets and fulfilled it, and she helped in the rehabilitation of Afghan refugees. Pakistan, a former colony of Britain, enjoys membership of the Commonwealth Organization; Britain helps in education and provides scholarships to hundreds of Pakistani students each year. Germany is one of the largest importers of Pakistani carpets, while Pakistan imports scientific equipment and electrical household appliances from Germany. Pakistan also has bilateral trade with other European Union members like Spain, Italy, Denmark, Norway and Belgium; the Norwegian mobile phone company Telenor has a vast network in Pakistan.

Key Points

  • America gave arms through SEATO (1954) and CENTO (1955) but did not help Pakistan in the 1965 and 1971 wars.
  • After 1979 America aided Pakistan against the Soviet invasion; after 11 September 2001 it offered one billion dollars.
  • Russia long favoured India and vetoed Kashmir resolutions, yet helped reconcile in 1965 (Tashkend Declaration) and funded Pakistan Steel Mills, Karachi.
  • Japan, an economic giant, is a major trade partner and aided Balochistan projects and Mohenjo Daro.
  • Britain gives scholarships through the Commonwealth link; France supplied Mirage jets in 1979.

lessons.title: Pakistan and the UNO
lessons.notes_html:
After World War-II, an international organization called the United Nations Organization (UNO) was founded on 26th October, 1945. Its purpose was to maintain peace in the world and resolve conflicts between nations through diplomatic means.

Pakistan Joins the UNO

Within a few months after independence, on 30th September, 1947, Pakistan became a member of the UNO. Pakistan made the UN Charter one of the important elements of her foreign policy and supports all UN policies. Pakistan has always taken an active part in eliminating apartheid policies from the world, under the UN Charter.

Pakistan's Services for the UNO

  • Pakistani experts have served the UNO at a high level: Sir Zafarullah Khan (Ex-Foreign Minister of Pakistan) served as the President of the General Assembly.
  • Whenever the UNO requested peacekeeping troops, Pakistan always responded positively. Pakistani peacekeeping troops and medical missions have rendered services in Somalia, Seraleon, Congo, etc.
  • Pakistan has always represented the Third World and Islamic countries in the General Assembly and rendered meritorious services in safeguarding their rights.
  • Pakistan moved many resolutions against Israeli aggression and led the Group-77, comprising the Third World Countries, in the General Assembly.
  • Pakistan has always supported the right of freedom for all nations according to the UNO Charter and supported politically and morally all independence movements throughout the world.

UNO, Kashmir and Pakistan

Pakistan accepts all the UNO resolutions regarding the Kashmir issue and always emphasised their implementation, but due to India's stubbornness this issue is still unresolved.

UNO Agencies Working in Pakistan

Different specialized agencies of the UNO have been working for the welfare of Pakistanis. Among them the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO), the United Nations International Children's Emergency Fund (UNICEF), the World Wildlife Fund (WWF) and the Food and Agricultural Organization (FAO) are worth mentioning.

Key Points

  • The UNO was founded on 26 October 1945 to maintain world peace through diplomatic means.
  • Pakistan became a member of the UNO on 30 September 1947.
  • Sir Zafarullah Khan served as President of the UN General Assembly.
  • Pakistani peacekeeping troops and medical missions served in Somalia, Seraleon and Congo.
  • Pakistan led the Group-77 and moved resolutions against Israeli aggression.
  • Pakistan accepts all UNO resolutions on Kashmir; UNESCO, UNICEF, WWF and FAO work in Pakistan.

lessons.title: Economic Development in Different Periods
lessons.notes_html:
At independence in 1947, Pakistan's economic sector was very weak. During British rule no major industries were set up in these areas. Lack of expertise and resources and poor administrative infrastructure created enormous economic challenges. After independence, reforms and Five Year Plans were made according to available resources.

First Five Year Plan (1955-60)

The Planning Board was set up in July 1953. The plan focused on raising the standard of living and increasing exports to improve the balance of payment. Housing, education, health and social welfare were given attention. Gross National Product (GNP) increased by 15%. The Industrial Development Corporation was established and Warsak Dam was founded with the cooperation of Canada.

Second Five Year Plan (1960-65)

Agriculture was given priority over industry. Canals and dams were constructed to improve irrigation. Water and power, communication, education and manpower also received attention. GNP increased by 38%, agricultural production by 27%, industrial production by 61% and exports reached 1,980 million rupees.

Third Five Year Plan (1965-70)

At its start, India waged war against Pakistan, so a large part of resources was spent on defence. Despite this, major projects like Tarbela Dam and Mangla Dam were completed.

Fourth Five Year Plan (1970-75)

Its aims were to speed up economic progress, raise per capita income and eliminate unemployment. Due to the Indo-Pak war of 1971, it could not be fully implemented and was later converted into an annual development plan.

Fifth Five Year Plan (1975-80)

The book states this plan started on 1st July, 1978. Its aims were basic needs, more employment and industrial development. GNP increased by 6% and industrial development by 9.7%. Steel Mills, Karachi started production, electricity was provided to 8,833 villages, communication increased by 20.2%, and food deficit changed into food surplus.

Sixth Five Year Plan (1983-88)

Launched from 1st July, 1983 for rapid and equally funded countrywide development. Electricity generation increased by 13.6%, oil and gas production by 11.8%, electricity reached 16,525 villages, 1,803 basic health units were founded and exports increased by 11%.

Seventh Five Year Plan (1988-93)

Aims included employment for educated youth, human resource development and basic amenities. It focused on payment of foreign loans, private sector development and price stability. It failed to achieve its targets; budget deficit increased, but private sector investment also increased.

Eighth Five Year Plan (1993-98)

Aimed at social and economic welfare, creation of 62 lacs new jobs and special projects for less developed areas. Agriculture production increased by 5.57%, a loan of Rs. 37 billion was granted to farmers and improved seeds were distributed. Industrial growth could not increase due to load shedding.

Medium Term Development Plan (2005-10)

After the 8th plan ended in June 1998, five year plans were halted due to instability of government, the nuclear test in 1998 and dismissal of the Nawaz Sharif Government. The Planning Commission then launched this plan to create a just and stable economic system, reduce poverty and develop energy, communication, education and public health. A long term National Energy Security Plan till 2030 was also devised: explore new reserves of oil, gas and coal; fully use existing resources to reduce dependence on oil; and encourage private sector investment in energy. At present, agriculture's share in GDP is 19.2%.

Key Points

  • In 1947 Pakistan's economy was very weak, with no major industries.
  • First Plan (1955-60): GNP +15%; Warsak Dam built with Canada's help.
  • Second Plan (1960-65) was the most successful: GNP +38%.
  • Third and Fourth Plans were disturbed by the wars of 1965 and 1971.
  • Fifth Plan: Steel Mills Karachi started; food deficit became food surplus.
  • Eighth Plan: Rs. 37 billion loan to farmers; industry hurt by load shedding.
  • Medium Term Plan (2005-10) aimed to reduce poverty and develop energy.

lessons.title: Sectors of Economy
lessons.notes_html:
The system of producing wealth (cash, commodity, energy etc.), its distribution and exchange is called economy. It has three basic sectors.

Three Sectors

SectorMeaningExamples
Primary SectorNatural raw materials are obtainedMining, agriculture, fisheries
Secondary SectorManufacturing activitiesIndustries making goods from raw material
Tertiary SectorTransportation and exchange of goods and servicesTrade, transport, bank services

Mining

Pakistan is rich in mineral resources. Up to 1947 only a few deposits were explored. Now the Geological Survey of Pakistan (GSP), Pakistan Mineral Development Corporation (PMDC) and foreign companies are exploiting them. The share of minerals in GDP (Gross Domestic Production) is 2.83%.

Types of Minerals

  • Basic Minerals: new products are made from them through a process; their own material existence is not eliminated, unlike coal and oil.
  • Power Minerals: they lose their entity after being used as fuel, e.g. coal, petroleum, gas and radioactive elements like uranium and plutonium.

Basic minerals are of two types: metallic and non-metallic.

Metallic Minerals

  • Chromite: chromium is extracted from it; used in making steel from iron and photographic equipment. Found in Muslimbagh, Chaghi and Kharan (Balochistan) and Malakand and Muhmand Agencies (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa). Pakistan is self-sufficient and exports it. The first metallurgical industry was set up in 2006-07.
  • Iron Ore: largest deposits at Sakesar and Kalabagh (Punjab); also at Langarhyal, Galdanin, Domal Nesar and Abbottabad (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa) and Kalat, Mangochar, Chilghazi, Nokundi, Khuzdar and Ziarat (Balochistan).
  • Copper: a precious metal; electric current passes easily through it, so power cables are made of it. Large deposits at Sandak, Rekodik and Amorie in Balochistan.
  • Gold and Silver: mostly used in jewellery; also found in the copper mines of Sandak and Rekodik.

Non-Metallic Minerals

  • Rock Salt: used in food, as preservative, and for baking soda and caustic soda. The Khewrha Mines of the Salt Range are famous and the oldest. Also at Warhcha (Khushab District) and Kalabagh, and glass-like transparent salt in Karak District.
  • Limestone: calcium carbonate; used for lime, bleaching powder, glass and cement. Huge deposits in the Salt Range and Margala Hills; also at Harnai, Makli, Kot Deji and Manghopir Hills.
  • Gypsum: used in cement, sculpturing, rubber, fertilizer and paper. Found in Karak, Mianwali, Jhelum, Dera Ghazi Khan, Khewrha, Quetta and Sibi.
  • Sulphur: acid is extracted from it; used in chemical and pharmaceutical industry, explosives, paints, fertilizers and matches. Found at Koh-e-Sultan (District Chaghi) and Sanni Shoran in Balochistan.
  • Marble: found in many colours; about 1200 million tonne identified deposits. Marble of Malagori area in Khyber Agency is considered the best in the world. Pakistan exports it in great quantity.
  • Gemstones: used in jewellery, e.g. emerald, sapphire, topaz, ruby.

Key Points

  • Economy has three sectors: primary, secondary (manufacturing) and tertiary (services).
  • Minerals share in GDP is 2.83%.
  • Basic minerals make new products; power minerals are used up as fuel.
  • Largest copper deposits: Sandak and Rekodik, Balochistan.
  • Khewrha salt mines are the oldest and most famous in Pakistan.
  • Pakistan has about 1200 million tonne of marble deposits.

lessons.title: Agriculture
lessons.notes_html:
The practice or science of growing crops is called agriculture. It is man's oldest occupation. People associated with farming often rear some animals as well.

Importance of Agriculture

Pakistan is a developing country and its economy is heavily dependent on agriculture. Approximately 55% of Pakistan's population is directly or indirectly associated with agriculture, and approximately 19.2% of GDP comes from agriculture. Most industrial units use raw material from the agricultural sector.

  • Food grains: wheat, rice, gram, corn, millet, sorghum, pulses and oil seeds. They fulfil the country's food requirements, and some industries use them as raw material.
  • Cash crops: cotton, sugarcane, tobacco and jute. They are used as raw material in many industries and are also exported.

Pakistan's irrigation system is quite extensive and modern. Where canals do not exist, irrigation is done through hill torrents, springs and wells/tubewells.

Agricultural Constraints

Pakistan has a variety of climate and fertile soil, and all major seasons prevail here, so a large variety of crops and vegetables is produced. Of the land under cultivation, 20% is rainfed while 80% is irrigated. Irrigation means supplying crops with water through artificial means, other than direct natural rain.

Population has increased rapidly since independence, so demand for food has also increased, but per acre yield is very low compared to many other countries. Factors responsible for low yield are:

  • Decreasing fertility of soil
  • Waterlogging and salinity
  • Use of traditional farming methods and substandard seeds
  • Dry climate and inadequate means of irrigation
  • Crop diseases
  • Lack of education and training in farmers

Reforms

To enhance the productivity of land, chemical fertilizer, modern machinery, agricultural medicines (pesticides) and improved seeds are being used. These reforms are described in detail in the lesson on Modern Agriculture.

Key Points

  • Agriculture is man's oldest occupation.
  • About 55% of the population is linked with agriculture; its share in GDP is 19.2%.
  • Food grains give food; cash crops like cotton and sugarcane give industry raw material and exports.
  • 80% of cultivated land is irrigated and 20% is rainfed.
  • Per acre yield is low due to salinity, traditional methods and poor seeds.
