lessons.title: Water Resources and Irrigation System
lessons.notes_html:
In most areas of Pakistan the climate is dry. About 80% of rain is received in midsummer. Sometimes rain causes floods, and at other times it is unreliable and insufficient, so rainfed agriculture is not successful. Pakistan's mountain ranges keep rainwater confined in narrow river beds, which can be dammed easily.

Indus Basin Treaty 1960

Through the mediation of the World Bank, Pakistan and India signed the Indus Basin Treaty in 1960. India got full rights over the three eastern rivers — Bias, Sutlej and Ravi. Pakistan got rights over the Indus and its two tributaries, Jehlum and Chenab.

Dams and Barrages

Pakistan has made the world's best irrigation system by building dams and barrages. The largest dams are Tarbela, Mangla and Warsak. Recently accomplished projects include Bhasha, Gomalzam, Mirani and Satpara dams. On the Indus, from Kalabagh down to its delta, five barrages have been constructed: Jinnah Barrage, Chashma Barrage, Taunsa Barrage, Guddu Barrage and Kotri or Sukkur Barrage. A few barrages are also built on Jehlum and Chenab.

Four Means of Irrigation

There are four means of irrigation in Pakistan: (i) Canals, (ii) Wells, (iii) Natural springs and karezes, (iv) Hill torrents. Canal networks are easy to develop in plain areas but very difficult in mountainous and plateau areas.

Canals

Our canal irrigation system is one of the best and vast systems of the world. Canals carry water from dams, barrages and headworks to the fields. There are three types:

  • Perennial Canals: water flows throughout the year, in both Rabi and Kharif seasons, e.g. Upper Chenab Canal, Lower Chenab Canal, Sidhnai Canal and Badian Canal.
  • Seasonal Canals: flow only in the rainy season or at the time of floods.
  • Link Canals: not meant to irrigate fields; they link one river with another or a canal with another canal, e.g. Marala-Ravi Canal, Qadirabad-Baloki Canal and Baloki-Sulemanki Canal.

Wells

  • Dugwells: dug into the earth in the form of broad ditches; water is lifted by a Persian Wheel or a motor-pipe system.
  • Tubewells: commonly called borings; installed in narrow deep bore holes with filter tubes (pipes); water is pumped out by surface mounted or submersible pumps.

Wells are used where canals are unavailable or insufficient. Well irrigation is more productive because it remains under the farmer's control, but it is a costly means compared to canals.

Natural Springs and Karezes

The point from where groundwater gushes out is called a natural spring. Artificial springs are called Karezes in Balochistan. The karez system is centuries old. First, a few wells are dug in a row in the foothills, called mother wells. Then they are joined by a tunnel, and the cumulative water is conveyed to the valley by an underground canal with openings at regular distances for light and aeration. Unless the mother wells dry out, a karez keeps flowing like a spring. In most areas of Balochistan karezes have dried out, but in Zhob, Loralai, Pishin, Quetta and Mastung Districts a few are still functioning.

Hill Torrents

When it rains, water from hill slopes accumulates to form rushing streams, which dry out as the rain stops. People block these torrents by constructing dikes to divert water to agricultural fields, one after another downslope. The dikes are constructed collectively by stakeholders. This method is popular in the hilly and rainfed areas and also enhances soil moisture.

Key Points

  • About 80% of rain falls in midsummer; rain is unreliable, so irrigation is essential.
  • Indus Basin Treaty 1960: eastern rivers to India; Indus, Jehlum and Chenab to Pakistan.
  • Largest dams: Tarbela, Mangla and Warsak.
  • Canals are of three types: perennial, seasonal and link canals.
  • A karez is an artificial spring in Balochistan made by joining mother wells with a tunnel.
  • Hill torrents are blocked by dikes to water fields in hilly, rainfed areas.

lessons.title: Crops
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan has two basic cropping seasons: (i) Rabi Season and (ii) Kharif Season. Crops cultivated in the Rabi Season are called Rabi Crops and those cultivated in the Kharif Season are called Kharif Crops.

Rabi and Kharif Crops

Rabi CropsKharif Crops
SeasonCultivated in October, harvested in AprilGrown from April to October
CropsBarley, gram, oil seeds and wheatCotton, millet, sorghum, corn, sugarcane and rice

Wheat

In wheat production, the Indus Plains have a lead over the rest of Pakistan. Wheat is cultivated on 75% of the under cultivation area in Punjab. In Sindh, wheat is cultivated on a large scale. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan, wheat is cultivated in small plain areas.

Rice

Pakistani rice is considered one of the best varieties in the world. Its cultivation requires a hot and humid climate. The climate of the northeast districts of Punjab — Sialkot, Sheikhopura and Gujranwala — is very suitable; rice of this region is of high quality, so most of its production is exported. Rice is also cultivated in Okara, Jhang, Narowal and Hafizabad. Naseerabad and Jaferabad Districts of Balochistan and Dera Ismail Khan District of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa also have a good share in rice cultivation.

Cotton

Cotton is another major crop of Pakistan. It is largely cultivated in the Indus Plains, including Dera Ghazi Khan, Multan, Khanewal and Bahawalpur Districts of Punjab and the interior districts of Sindh. It is also grown in Dera Ismail Khan, Mardan and Peshawar Districts of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Loralai and Lasbela Districts of Balochistan.

Key Points

  • Two seasons: Rabi (October to April) and Kharif (April to October).
  • Rabi crops: wheat, barley, gram, oil seeds.
  • Kharif crops: cotton, rice, sugarcane, corn, millet, sorghum.
  • Wheat covers 75% of the cultivated area in Punjab.
  • Best rice areas: Sialkot, Sheikhopura and Gujranwala; most of it is exported.
  • Cotton is mainly grown in the Indus Plains of Punjab and Sindh.

lessons.title: Fishing
lessons.notes_html:
Although fishing adds only 0.4 percent to the GDP of Pakistan, lacs of people are engaged in this occupation. Pakistan has two sources of fishing: (i) Sea and (ii) Rivers.

Sea Fishing

Sea fishing is practised in the coastal belts of Sindh and Balochistan Provinces. The coast of Sindh has a lead over Balochistan's coast in fish yield, because the River Indus carries a lot of fish towards the sea. In the open sea, fishing is done through large modern ships. The bulk of our fish catch is exported.

River Fishing

This fishing is carried out in rivers, dams, natural lakes, canals and ponds. The fish catch in the rivers and lakes of Sindh is larger than that of Punjab. The River Indus is the biggest source of fishing in Sindh. Lake Manchher, Lake Kinchher and Chotyari Dam (Sangarh) are also famous sites. A good amount of fish is also obtained from Mangla Dam and Chashma Barrage in Punjab. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, fish is caught from Tarbela Dam, Warsak Dam, Tanda Dam (Kohat) and Baran Dam (Bannu).

Fish farming is also in practice in Pakistan. People build private fish farms, where better varieties are produced.

Key Points

  • Fishing contributes only 0.4% to GDP but employs lacs of people.
  • Two sources: sea fishing and river fishing.
  • Sindh's coast gives more fish than Balochistan's coast; most sea catch is exported.
  • Famous river fishing sites: River Indus, Lake Manchher, Lake Kinchher and Chotyari Dam.
  • Private fish farms produce better varieties of fish.

lessons.title: Modern Agriculture
lessons.notes_html:
About 43.7% of Pakistan's labour force is engaged in agriculture. Despite this, the actual problem of Pakistan's agriculture is its low productivity, which is lower than that of developed countries due to various constraints. The Government has taken many steps to increase agricultural productivity.

Use of Chemical Fertilizer

High-yield crops require greater feed, which chemical fertilizer only can provide. In Pakistan during 2017-18, production of chemical fertilizers was 6 million metric tonne and 0.1 million metric tonne was imported. The government gives subsidy on its price, and agricultural banks provide loans at a low rate of interest for its purchase.

Use of Machinery

Traditional methods — ploughing, sowing and threshing by animals and harvesting with hand sickle — do not help cultivate land on a large scale and cause huge loss to the harvest. Modern machinery solves these problems. The use of the tractor is now common; with special machinery attached, it also helps in sowing, harvesting and threshing. The government encourages modern machinery by reducing import taxes on it and has granted incentives for indigenously manufacturing agricultural machinery. Presently, there are three tractor manufacturing factories in the country. The Agricultural Development Bank grants soft loans to farmers for the purchase of fertilizer and tractors.

Use of Agricultural Medicines

Like animals, plants also have diseases. Diseases and insects cause 20% loss to crop yield. Farmers now use pesticides and insecticides, although they are poisonous and cause harm to human health. It is essential to cultivate crops which have strong resistance power against diseases.

Use of Improved Seeds

Improved seeds show resistance against diseases and give high yield. An organization operates laboratories at about 17 areas of different climates all over the country to improve seeds. Seed corporations are active in all provinces, and international companies also provide improved seeds. The responsibility of production and distribution of seeds is entrusted to the Agricultural Development Corporation. There are four government organizations working for the supply of seeds, besides many private companies preparing quality seeds.

More Government Steps

  • Dam and canal construction projects are underway to increase water supply for irrigation.
  • Two departments purchase crops directly from farmers at fixed rates: Agricultural Marketing and Storage Limited and Pakistan Agricultural Storage and Services Corporation. The Utility Stores Corporation also purchases crops directly from farmers.
  • For agricultural research, Agriculture Research Farms, Agriculture Universities and Colleges and Agriculture Research Councils have been established, where research is conducted on seed culturing and crop diseases.

Key Points

  • 43.7% of the labour force works in agriculture, but productivity is low.
  • Fertilizer production in 2017-18 was 6 million metric tonne; government gives subsidy on it.
  • Diseases and insects cause 20% loss to crop yield.
  • There are three tractor factories; the Agricultural Development Bank gives soft loans.
  • Improved seeds are tested in laboratories at about 17 areas of the country.

lessons.title: Agricultural Problems
lessons.notes_html:
A large segment of Pakistan's population is associated with agriculture, yet we are not self-sufficient in many staple crops. The following problems are responsible for this deficiency.

Main Problems

  • Illiteracy of farmers: The majority of our farmers are illiterate, whereas education is very significant in this profession. An educated farmer can better understand the right time of cultivation, the right amount of irrigation, the use of suitable fertilizer and pesticides and the use of modern agricultural machinery.
  • Poverty of farmers: Most farmers are poor. They can spare little from the income of one season's crop to invest in the next season's crop, so the chances of getting a good yield are minimal.
  • Rare use of modern technology: The use of modern technology is rare. Neither do the farmers know how to use it, nor can they afford to buy it.
  • Fragmentation of land: Agricultural land per farmer has reduced due to its fragmentation under inheritance rules. This puts a big hurdle in the application of modern agricultural techniques.
  • Political instability: Powerful countries can easily export their surplus to international markets, whereas our farmers find it impossible to have access to international markets. They feel worried about access to markets, especially in the case of fast perishing products.

Other causes of low yield noted earlier in the chapter include decreasing fertility of soil, waterlogging and salinity, traditional farming methods, substandard seeds, dry climate, inadequate means of irrigation and crop diseases.

Key Points

  • Pakistan is not self-sufficient in many staple crops despite a large farming population.
  • Most farmers are illiterate and poor, so they cannot use or afford modern methods.
  • Land is divided into small pieces under inheritance rules, blocking modern techniques.
  • Political instability and lack of access to international markets hurt farmers.
  • Waterlogging, salinity and crop diseases further reduce yield.

mcqs.why: A large segment of Pakistan's population is associated with agriculture, yet we are not self-sufficient in many staple crops, due to problems like illiteracy and poverty of farmers.

mcqs.why: Other causes of low yield include decreasing fertility of soil, waterlogging and salinity, traditional farming methods, substandard seeds, dry climate, inadequate irrigation and crop diseases.

mcqs.why: Fragmentation of land under inheritance rules puts a big hurdle in the application of modern agricultural techniques, because very small pieces cannot be farmed with modern machinery economically.

mcqs.why: Farmers feel worried about access to markets, especially in the case of fast perishing products, which spoil quickly if not sold in time.

mcqs.why: The majority of our farmers are illiterate, whereas education is very significant in this profession — this is listed first among the main agricultural problems.

lessons.title: Industries
lessons.notes_html:
Next to agriculture, industry is the other most important sector of our economy, and the economic progress of the country depends upon progress in this sector. Industry helps to:

  • Increase job opportunities
  • Increase the volume of exports
  • Increase the reserves of foreign exchange
  • Stabilize and broaden the bases of economy
  • Export agricultural production in value added (manufactured) form instead of raw form

Agricultural development is linked to industrial development, because industry provides agricultural equipment, fertilizers, pesticides/insecticides, transportation vehicles and machinery for value addition to raw agricultural products. The industry of Pakistan is classified into three types.

Cottage Industry

It is set up in homes and markets in small simple buildings and is mostly run with muscle power. Workers buy raw material from local markets and sell finished goods in the same markets. Examples: tailoring, embroidery, black smithy, carpentry, shoe making, flour mills and bakeries. Other products include wood work, iron work, jewellery work, carpet weaving, furniture making, cane work in baskets, clay pots, glass, bangles, fireworks, toys and decoration pieces. There is hardly any village or city without a cottage industry suited to the local culture. Better communication has introduced these products to the international market; foreign tourists take keen interest in them, and the government has established expo centers in several cities where tourists purchase items of their interest.

Small Industry

Small and large industry are differentiated by capital invested, number of employees and nature of energy used. By the latest definition, a small industry is one where capital investment ranges from 10 million to 100 million rupees, and the number of employees is small. Factories of sports goods, surgical equipment, medicines and carpets fall in this category. Most of the private sector industry in Pakistan is small industry, and these are the major employers of the country's workforce. This industry is very common in Lahore, Gujranwala, Faisalabad and Sialkot, and industrial zones in the suburbs of almost every big city are dominated by it. It faces many hurdles, and the government must pay attention so that employment increases and raw material is turned into finished products.

Large Industry

In large industry, capital investment exceeds Rs. 100 million and the number of employees is quite large. This type is rapidly growing in Pakistan. Examples: big textile mills, mechanical complexes, sugar mills, fertilizer factories, cement factories, iron and steel mills and oil refineries. Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad, Multan and Sialkot are famous for having large industrial units.

Key Points

  • Industry increases jobs, exports and foreign exchange reserves.
  • Industry and agriculture support each other.
  • Cottage industry: run in homes with muscle power, e.g. embroidery, carpet weaving, pottery.
  • Small industry: investment of 10 million to 100 million rupees; major employer of the workforce.
  • Large industry: investment above Rs. 100 million, e.g. textile mills, steel mills, oil refineries.
  • Famous industrial cities: Karachi, Lahore, Faisalabad, Multan and Sialkot.

mcqs.why: Industry helps to increase job opportunities, increase the volume of exports, increase the reserves of foreign exchange, stabilize the economy, and export agricultural production in value added form.

mcqs.why: Cottage industry products include wood work, iron work, jewellery work, carpet weaving, furniture making, cane work in baskets, clay pots, glass and bangles; surgical equipment factories fall in small industry.

lessons.title: Energy Resource
lessons.notes_html:
Energy resources are vital for economic development. Countries that used them properly, like the USA, France, Britain and Germany, progressed fast. Oil and gas brought great development to Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. In Pakistan, Sui gas exploration has saved foreign exchange worth billions of rupees.

Hydroelectricity

Electricity produced by the kinetic force of flowing water; waterfalls run the machines called turbines, and artificial waterfalls are created on dams. It rose from 68 MW in 1947 to 6,670 MW by 2014. Main users: domestic, industrial and agricultural sectors.

DamFacts
Tarbela (River Indus)World's largest earth-filled dam; built 1968–1976; 3,478 MW; also for irrigation
Mangla (River Jhelum)Second largest source; completed 1967; 1,000 MW
Warsak (River Kabul)Started 1952 with help of Canada; completed in phases 1960–1981; 240 MW; irrigates about 20 thousand acres
Ghazi Barotha (River Indus)Producing since June 2004; 1,450 MW

Thermal Electricity

Water is boiled by burning coal, oil or gas; the steam pressure runs the generators. These plants serve big cities and substitute hydroelectricity when its supply fails. KESCO built many plants for Karachi; WAPDA built them at Hyderabad, Sukkar, Jamshoro, Guddu (Sindh), Rawalpindi, Lahore, Faisalabad, Kot Addu, Muzafargarh, Multan (Punjab) and Quetta, Pasni, Hub (Balochistan).

Nuclear Electricity

Started in 1971 with the first plant at Karachi, set up with Canada's cooperation — capacity 137 MW. The second plant at Chashma near Mianwali generates 300 MW.

Natural Gas

Also called fuel gas; after electricity it is the largest energy source. It is clean and easy to use. First explored at Sui (Balochistan) in 1952, hence called Sui Gas. It meets one-third of energy needs — used as house fuel, heavily by the fertilizer industry, and in vehicles as CNG. Reserves: Balochistan — Sui, Pirkoh, Zin, Uch; Punjab — Dharnal, Toot, Dhulian, Mial, Dhodak; Sindh — Sari, Mari, Kandkot, Khanpur, Hundi, Mazarani; Khyber Pakhtunkhwa — Kohat and Karak.

Coal

Pakistani coal is of low quality, used in houses and brick kilns. Mining started in 1887; coal is produced in all four provinces. Punjab: Makarwal, Dandot, Pidh, Kalabagh. Balochistan: Sorange, Khost, Shahreg, Harnai, Chamalang, Degari, Dukki, Mach — better quality, also used in Pakistan Steel Mills, Karachi. Sindh gives almost 90% of production — Lakhra, Jhempir, Meting and Thar (explored 1992; projects underway to generate electricity from it). Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Kohat and Darra Adam Khel (Orakzai Agency).

Mineral Oil

Petroleum, called liquid gold, is mainly used in aeroplanes, vehicles and some industries. The biggest producing region is the Potohar Plateau (Dhulian, Khore, Mial, Balkasar, Joyameer, Sarang). Reserves also exist at Dhodak (D.G. Khan) and Khaskheli (Badin). Local reserves are insufficient, so oil is imported. Refineries: Pakistan Oil Refinery and National Oil Refinery at Karachi, and one at Mahmood Kot for Dhodak crude oil.

Non-Conventional Resources

Conventional resources will not last long, so bio-gas, solar, wind and tidal energy are being explored. Solar energy is very useful and cheap; solar plants produce 135 KW. Bio-gas is made by decomposing animals' dung in special plants. In coastal Balochistan and Sindh, wind power runs grinding mills and water pumps.

Key Points

  • Proper use of energy resources is essential for economic progress.
  • Hydroelectricity: 68 MW (1947) to 6,670 MW (2014); Tarbela is largest at 3,478 MW.
  • Nuclear plants: Karachi 137 MW, Chashma 300 MW.
  • Natural gas from Sui (1952) meets one-third of energy needs; Sindh gives 90% of coal.
  • Petroleum is liquid gold; solar, bio-gas, wind and tidal are non-conventional resources.

mcqs.why: Hydroelectricity, produced by the kinetic force of flowing water running turbines, rose from 68 MW in 1947 to 6,670 MW by 2014; its main users are the domestic, industrial and agricultural sectors.

mcqs.why: Tarbela on the River Indus is the world's largest earth-filled dam, built 1968-1976, with 3,478 MW capacity; Mangla gives 1,000 MW, Warsak 240 MW and Ghazi Barotha 1,450 MW — together 3478 + 1000 + 240 + 1450 = 6,168 MW.

mcqs.why: Warsak Dam on the River Kabul was started in 1952 with the help of Canada and completed in phases 1960-1981; it produces 240 MW and irrigates about 20 thousand acres.

mcqs.why: Nuclear electricity started in 1971 with the first plant at Karachi, set up with Canada's cooperation, with a capacity of 137 MW; the second plant at Chashma near Mianwali generates 300 MW.

mcqs.why: Natural gas, after electricity the largest energy source, meets one-third of energy needs; reserves exist in Balochistan (Sui, Pirkoh, Uch), Punjab, Sindh and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.

mcqs.why: Sindh gives almost 90% of coal production — from Lakhra, Jhempir, Meting and Thar; Thar was explored in 1992 and projects are underway to generate electricity from it.

mcqs.why: The biggest petroleum producing region is the Potohar Plateau (Dhulian, Khore, Mial, Balkasar, Joyameer, Sarang); reserves also exist at Dhodak and Khaskheli, but local reserves are insufficient so oil is imported.

mcqs.why: Among non-conventional resources, solar energy is very useful and cheap and solar plants produce 135 KW; bio-gas is made from animals' dung and wind power is used in coastal Balochistan and Sindh.

lessons.title: Foreign Trade
lessons.notes_html:
The activity of selling and buying goods is called trade. If it is conducted with other countries, it is called foreign or international trade. The book gives four important factors that influence international trade.

Foreign Policy

Friendly relations promote trade links. Pakistan has strong trade relations with Muslim Arab countries because of strong spiritual and political affiliations with them. On the other hand, Pakistan has never enjoyed good relations with India; therefore, despite being close neighbours, trade relations could not be promoted with her.

Means of Transportation

For smooth foreign trade, a country must have reliable means of transportation. Pakistan has land, sea and air links with all important countries of the world. We are not dependent on any other country for the means of transportation required for our international trade.

Tariff

The volume of trade between any two countries depends on their tariff rates. Friendly countries levy low tariff on the imports and exports of one another. As a result, their goods become cheaper and are able to compete in the market.

Political Stability

Political stability and investment go hand in hand. If a country undergoes political instability, not only foreign investors but also local investors hesitate to invest there.

Key Points

  • Buying and selling of goods is trade; trade with other countries is foreign trade.
  • Friendly foreign policy promotes trade, as with the Muslim Arab countries.
  • Pakistan has land, sea and air links with all important countries.
  • Low tariff between friendly countries makes goods cheaper and competitive.
  • Political instability discourages both foreign and local investors.

lessons.title: Imports and Exports
lessons.notes_html:
International trade has two types: imports and exports. Items brought from other countries are imports. Pakistan has enough natural resources but is industrially backward, so it imports machinery, and it is not self-sufficient in some minerals and crops.

Major Imports

  • Industrial Machinery: we lack technology to make industrial machinery, so machinery and scientific equipment come from Europe, Northern America, Australia, Japan and China.
  • Transport Machinery: aeroplanes, ships, trains, buses, trucks, cars and motor cycles, from the same countries.
  • Defense Equipment: despite our own ordnance factories, sophisticated weapons are bought from China, USA, Russia and European countries.
  • Iron and Steel: for machinery spare parts; local production is insufficient — imported from USA, Japan, Germany and UK.
  • Medicines and Chemical Compounds: from Germany, France, Italy, USA and Japan.
  • Agricultural Products: soybean oil from USA, palm oil from Malaysia, tea from Kenya, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, wheat from USA and Australia. Also paper, electronics, cosmetics and sports goods.

Exports

Goods produced at home and sold to foreign countries are exports. Pakistan's export base is narrow — food cereals, cotton, wool, leather, some minerals and a few simple products.

  • Cotton Products: raw cotton, yarn, cloth and readymade garments to Hong Kong, Japan, Bangladesh, Middle-East, USA, China, Germany, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.
  • Hide, Leather and Wool: raw and finished, to Iran, Russia, Spain, Italy and Japan.
  • Handicrafts: embroidered garments, marble decoration pieces, metallic utensils and sports goods — earn much foreign exchange.
  • Carpets and Mats: liked worldwide for beauty and durability — to rich Arab countries, Germany and America.
  • Rice and Fish: surplus items; high quality basmati rice to Middle-East, Europe and some African countries; fish mostly to the Middle-East. Also readymade garments, surgical tools, fruits, vegetables, tobacco and unrefined sugar (gurh).

Key Points

  • Imports = goods brought in; exports = home goods sold abroad.
  • Main imports: machinery, transport and defense equipment, iron and steel, medicines, chemicals, edible oil, tea and wheat.
  • Main exports: cotton products, leather, wool, handicrafts, carpets, rice and fish.
  • Pakistan's export base is narrow and based on simple products.

mcqs.why: International trade has two types: items brought from other countries are imports, while goods produced at home and sold to foreign countries are exports.

mcqs.why: We lack technology to make industrial machinery, so machinery and scientific equipment come from Europe, Northern America, Australia, Japan and China.

mcqs.why: Among agricultural imports, soybean oil comes from the USA, palm oil from Malaysia, tea from Kenya, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka, and wheat from the USA and Australia.

mcqs.why: Tea is imported from Kenya, Bangladesh and Sri Lanka; Pakistan also imports paper, electronics, cosmetics and sports goods.

mcqs.why: Pakistan's export base is narrow — food cereals, cotton, wool, leather, some minerals and a few simple products; cotton products go to Hong Kong, Japan, the Middle-East, USA, China and others.

mcqs.why: Handicrafts — embroidered garments, marble decoration pieces, metallic utensils and sports goods — earn much foreign exchange for Pakistan.

lessons.title: Trade Balance
lessons.notes_html:
Balance of trade means the proportion between the volume of imports and exports. If the volumes are not equal, the trade is called imbalanced trade. If expenditure on imports is more than the profit earned from exports, it is called trade deficit.

Pakistan's Position

Pakistan's economy is based on the production and export of raw material, while we import expensive finished products. That is why our overall foreign trade is imbalanced.

Trade partnersBalance for Pakistan
European countries — UK, Germany, France, Norway, Sweden, BelgiumNegative — we earn less foreign exchange from exports but pay more for imports
East European countries — Greece, Hungry, Poland, RomaniaPositive — we export more goods to them than we import from them
Middle-East countriesIn our favour — we import petroleum and dates from them and export agricultural commodities, arms, garments and carpets; export value is more than import value
Asian countries — China, Russia, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Sri Lanka, Bangladesh — and North American countries — USA and CanadaWe face trade deficit

How the Gap Is Bridged

Every year we have a trade deficit in our budget. To bridge this gap, taxes are increased and foreign loans are obtained. Remittances from overseas Pakistanis also help a lot in compensating the foreign trade deficit. This means the share of manpower export is significant in the export trade of Pakistan.

Key Points

  • Balance of trade is the proportion between imports and exports.
  • Spending more on imports than earning from exports is a trade deficit.
  • Pakistan exports raw material and imports expensive finished products, so its trade is imbalanced.
  • Trade balance is negative with Western Europe and in deficit with Asia and North America, but positive with East Europe and in our favour with the Middle-East.
  • The gap is bridged by higher taxes, foreign loans and remittances of overseas Pakistanis.

mcqs.q: Balance of trade means:
options: The proportion between the volume of imports and exports
mcqs.why: Balance of trade means the proportion between the volume of imports and exports; if the volumes are not equal, the trade is called imbalanced trade.

options: Expenditure on imports is more than the profit earned from exports
mcqs.why: If expenditure on imports is more than the profit earned from exports, it is called trade deficit; Pakistan faces this because it exports raw material and imports expensive finished products.

lessons.title: Sea Ports
lessons.notes_html:
A place where ships are anchored and heavy goods are loaded or unloaded is called a sea-port. Ships were once used for passengers, like Hajj travels, but with more air traffic, ship voyages have almost ended. Pakistan has three major sea-ports.

Sea-portImportant facts
Kimari (Karachi)Natural port with all anchoring facilities. Handled 3.5 million tonnes in 1947-48, rising to 26 million tonnes in 2017-18.
Port Bin QasimOn Gharo Creek, about 20 km southeast of Karachi; built in 1980 mainly for Pakistan Steel Mills; an industrial estate nearby has textile, chemicals, cement and leather factories.
Gawadar (Gwadar)On the Balochistan coast; important for its strategic location. Construction started 2001 with China's collaboration; working since 2009; master plan area 2,500 acres.

CPEC

On 20th April 2015 the Chinese President announced the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC) in Islamabad and signed investment agreements worth 46.5 billion dollars. Kashghar will be linked to Gwadar by highway and railway till 2030, making Pakistan important in economy, defense and as a trade route.

Dry Ports

Pakistan has six dry ports, run by Pakistan Railway. The first was established in 1973 at Mughalpura Railway Station, Lahore; others are at Karachi, Quetta, Peshawar, Multan and Rawalpindi. Imports received at Karachi Port are carried by railway to dry ports, where importers collect them — so traders can handle imports and exports from their own city.

Key Points

  • Three major sea-ports: Kimari, Port Bin Qasim and Gawadar.
  • Kimari handled 26 million tonnes in 2017-18; Bin Qasim (1980) serves Pakistan Steel Mills.
  • Gwadar has worked since 2009, built with China's collaboration.
  • CPEC (2015) brings 46.5 billion dollars of agreements and links Kashghar to Gwadar by 2030.
  • Six dry ports are run by Pakistan Railway; the first opened at Lahore in 1973.

lessons.title: Poverty
lessons.notes_html:
Poverty means the lack of production and per capita income in a country, which results in lack of saving and investment and keeps the living standard of people low.

Ratio and Poverty Line

About one-fourth (25%) of Pakistan's people live below the Poverty Line — the minimum income level, below two US dollars daily, at which a person cannot meet the basic needs of life. The majority of Pakistanis earn less than two dollars a day.

Causes of Poverty

  • Population growth is much faster than the growth of resources and production.
  • Costly farming: over 63% of people live in rural areas and depend on agriculture; machines, pesticides, improved seeds and chemical fertilizers are expensive imports, and farmers often get poor prices for their yields.
  • Land fragmentation: under Inheritance Laws, land is divided into smaller pieces; small farmers cannot live on farming alone.
  • Weak industry: a backward industrial base means fewer job opportunities.
  • Corruption: corruption, smuggling, hoarding, bribery and tax evasion affect all fields of life.
  • Political instability: unstable politics, discontinuous policies and law and order problems drive capital out and cause unemployment.
  • Feudalism: feudals deprive poor farmers of their due share and fair wages.

Consequences

Poverty brings political instability, internal and external threats, and crime and law and order problems. Most people lack balanced food and medical facilities, and the poor cannot educate their children — so people remain illiterate, unskilled, physically sick and discouraged.

Preventive Measures

Governments encouraged foreign investment and jobs. The Food Support Programme, Khushhal Pakistan Programme, Pakistan Rural Support Programme and Benazir Income Support Programme helped little. Essential steps: birth control, proper planning, equitable resource distribution, standard educational facilities, more use of modern technology and private sector development.

Key Points

  • About 25% of Pakistanis live below the Poverty Line of two US dollars a day.
  • Causes: fast population growth, costly farming, land fragmentation, weak industry, corruption, instability and feudalism.
  • Poverty causes crime, illiteracy, poor food and health.
  • Support programmes helped little; planning, education, fair distribution and technology are essential.

lessons.title: Population
lessons.notes_html:
Population means "the total number of people living in a particular area". Knowing the size and composition of population is essential for future planning. The Population Census Organization conducts a census after every 10 years. The first census of Pakistan was held in 1951, and five more censuses followed.

Growth of Population

Population grows for two reasons: net migration (immigrants coming in minus emigrants going out) and the excess of births over deaths. Movement inside the country does not change the total, but international migration does. Pakistan's population rose rapidly at Partition, when Muslims migrated from India. The annual growth rate was highest at 3.67% in 1972, then declined to 2.69% in 1998 and 2.4% in 2017.

Distribution and Density

Population distribution in Pakistan is quite uneven because of diversified terrain, climatic differences and uneven distribution of economic resources. According to the 2017 census:

  • Punjab 52.9% of the population on only 26% of the area - its plain terrain, developed agriculture and extensive irrigation system attract people.
  • Sindh 23%, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 17.1%, Islamabad 0.69%.
  • Balochistan is the largest province, covering nearly 44% of the area, but has only 5.9% of the population because of unfavourable physical conditions.

Population density is the number of people per square kilometre. In 2017 it was 261 persons per sq. km for Pakistan: Punjab 533, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 349, Sindh 340 and Balochistan 36.

Rural-Urban Ratio

The rural-urban ratio shows whether the primary sector (agriculture, livestock) or industry dominates. Pakistan is an agricultural country, so most people live in villages, but the urban share keeps rising: rural/urban was 82.4% / 17.6% in 1951, 67.5% / 32.5% in 1998, and 63.6% / 36.4% in 2017.

Sex Ratio

In the 2017 census, out of 207.8 million people, 106.4 million were males and 101.3 million were females. The overall sex ratio was 106, i.e. 106 males for every 100 females. Province-wise it was: Punjab 107.23, Sindh 112.24, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 105.1 and Balochistan 114.61. Migration is the most important factor in sex-ratio variation.

Key Points

  • First census 1951 (33.7 million); population reached 207.8 million in 2017.
  • Growth rate fell from 3.67% (1972) to 2.4% (2017).
  • Distribution is uneven: Punjab 52.9%, Balochistan only 5.9% on 44% of the area.
  • Density 2017: Pakistan 261, Punjab 533, Balochistan 36 persons per sq. km.
  • Rural/urban in 2017: 63.6% / 36.4%; in 1998 the urban share was 32.5%.
  • Sex ratio 2017: 106 males per 100 females.

lessons.title: Society and Culture of Pakistan
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistani society is an Islamic society: belief in the oneness of Allah and in Muhammad (peace be upon him) as the last Rasool binds the people together despite ethnic and linguistic differences. Urdu is the national language; regional languages include Punjabi, Saraiki, Balochi, Brahui, Pashto, Sindhi and Potohari. Most people work in agriculture. The common dress is Shalwar Kameez; main foods are wheat bread, rice, vegetables, meat and pulses. Religious festivals are Eid-ul-Fitr, Eid-ul-Azha, Shab-e-Baraat and Eid Milad-un-Nabi; Hindus celebrate Diwali and Christians Christmas with full freedom. National days include Pakistan Day, Independence Day, Quaid-e-Azam Day and Allama Iqbal Day.

Challenges to Pakistani Society

  • Illiteracy - blocks progress and creates provincial, lingual and sectarian prejudices.
  • Over-population - growth beyond available resources causes poverty, inflation and unemployment.
  • Poverty - people cannot meet the basic needs of life.
  • Begging - beggars crowd streets, markets, hospitals and stations, and spread crime and disease.
  • Use of drugs - forbidden in Islam, yet spreading fast, especially among the youth.
  • Child labour - children under fourteen work in hotels, workshops, factories and brick kilns, though the law bans it.

Literacy and Education

Literacy is the simple ability to read and write; the 1998 census defined a literate person as one who can read newspapers and write simple letters in any language. Education is a formal process with curriculum, examinations and certificates - every educated person is literate, but every literate person is not educated. Literacy rose from 44% in 1998 to 62% in 2017 (2017: Punjab 64.7%, Sindh 62.2%, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa 55.3%, Balochistan 55.5%). Education is informal (skills like embroidery, driving, typing, training of farmers) or formal, which has four levels: Primary (first five years; education is compulsory and free up to class 10), Secondary (classes 6-10), Higher Secondary (two years: F.Sc. science, F.A. arts) and Higher Education (B.A., B.Sc., M.A., M.Sc., M.Phil, Ph.D; helped by the Higher Education Commission - HEC). Educational problems: medium of instruction (over-priority to English), outdated examination system (tests memory only), untrained teachers and lack of coordination between teachers and parents.

Public Health: Problems

The death rate, especially of women and children, is high despite malaria and smallpox eradication, immunization and polio programmes, Basic Health Units, hospitals and medical colleges. Main problems: poor diet (adulterated and impure food), polluted water (no clean drinking water or proper sewerage), poor housing (narrow, unventilated one- or two-room houses), unhygienic conditions (garbage piles, germs, mosquitoes), lack of health facilities and substandard medicines, and environmental pollution (factory waste, vehicle smoke, cutting of trees - causing heart, lungs and skin diseases; tree plantation helps).

Society and Culture

Living together is called society. Culture is the pattern of living practiced in a community for centuries - the manners prevailing in a society over ages - also called customs and traditions. "Culture is the way of life which a society develops generation after generation in the light of its material and spiritual needs." Pakistani culture dominantly reflects Islamic teachings: before Islam, Arabs served guests with wine and music, but after accepting Islam they abandoned such practices. Pakistan's land - lofty mountains, plateaus, vast plains and an about 1050 km coastal belt - gives each region its own way of life.

National Culture

  • Ethical values - Islamic brotherhood and equality, respect for elders and aged parents, respect for women, rights of neighbours.
  • Festivals - the two Eids; Pakistan Day (23rd March), Independence Day (14th August), Defence Day (6th September), Iqbal and Quaid-e-Azam days.
  • Architecture - began with Mohammad Bin Qasim (712 A.D.): Badshahi Masjid, Shahi Qilaa, Shalimar Garden, Sunehri Masjid (Lahore), Masjid Mohabbat Khan (Peshawar), Masjid Shah Jahan (Thatta), Masjid Bhong (Sadiqabad).
  • Calligraphy - developed under the Mughals; Babar, Aurangzeb Alamgeer, Bahadar Shah Zafar practiced it; Sadiqain and Gul Jee are Pakistan's prominent names.
  • Dresses - shalwar kameez; women wear dopatta; rural Punjab wears tehband; Sindhis wear embroidered caps and Ajrak; Pashtoons wear waistcoat and turban or Qaraqulli cap; Baloch women wear thickly embroidered dresses.
  • Food - wheat and rice are staple, corn in Kashmir and the Northern Areas; Islam divides food into Halal and Haram; fish in coastal areas; dry fruits in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan.

Regional Cultures

  • Balochistan - cordial, hospitable people; tribal feelings, respect for elders; women's embroidery, woollen carpets and tents; folklore Hani-Shah Murid.
  • Punjab - hardworking; fond of kabaddi and wrestling; folk tales Sassi-Punnu, Heer-Ranjha, Sohni-Mahinwal; enameling, sports goods, kite making.
  • Khyber Pakhtunkhwa - brave, hardworking, hospitable; embroidery, woollen clothes, carpet weaving, carved wooden goods.
  • Sindh - world-famous handicrafts, embroidery, earthen pottery, tile painting; agriculture main occupation; horse and oxen races.

All regions share common traits that create national solidarity: Islam, respect for humanity and women, Urdu, the Masjid and other religious institutions, similar customs of worship, hospitality and neighbours' rights, the same festivals, and the shalwar kameez dress.

Languages

English is the official language, Urdu the national language. Urdu comes from a Turkish word meaning "Army"; it formed among soldiers of different areas in the Mughal period, was called Hindwi, then Reekhta, then Urdu-e-Mualla, and finally Urdu. Pioneer poets: Ameer Khusro, Qulli Qutub Shah, Wali Dakni; great poets: Mir Taqi Mir, Asadullah Khan Ghalib, Khwaja Mir Dard, Khwaja Haider Ali Atish. Sir Syed Ahmad Khan's Aligarh College, Maulana Altaf Hussain Hali, Baba-e-Urdu Maulvi Abdul Haq, Maulana Shibli Noamani and Deputy Nazir Ahmed promoted it; much of Allama Iqbal's poetry is in Urdu.

  • Balochi - language of the Baloch tribes, linked to Iranian languages of Aryan times. Dialects: Eastern/Sulaimani, Rakhshani and Western (shows Persian influence). Classical poets include Mir Chakar Khan Rind and Sheh Murid. Balochi Deewan composed in 1951; Balochi Academy established in 1959.
  • Pashto - ancient Indo-Aryan language of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and northern Balochistan; soft western and tough eastern dialects, Kandahari the most moderate. First book "Pata Khazana" (8th century A.D.); first poet Ameer Karor. Khushal Khan Khattak (1613-1691) wrote on mysticism, morality and bravery; Rahman Baba is the famous Sufi poet of Pashto, whose main theme is mysticism. Pashto Academy set up in Peshawar in 1954.
  • Brahui - ancient language linked to the Dravidian languages; spoken in Bolan, Sarawan, Jhalawan and Makran; written in Persio-Arabic script; four dialects - Sarawani, Jhalawani, Noshkai, Sindhi. Folk story "Laili Moor"; Malik Dad's "Tuhfa-tul-Ajaib" is its first authentic book; Brahui Academy is in Quetta.
  • Sindhi - derived from Turkish, Dravidian and Sanskrit; standard dialect "Sahtee". Mystical poetry made it popular: Shah Abdul Latif Bhitai ("Shah Jo Resalo"), Hazrat Sachal Sarmast, Shah Inayat Shaheed.
  • Punjabi - six dialects; Majhi is the most popular (northern Punjab, Lahore). Sufi poets: Baba Farid Ganj-e-Shakar, Shah Hussain, Sultan Bahu, Bhullay Shah, Waris Shah, Khwaja Ghulam Farid, Hazrat Mian Muhammad Bakhsh.
  • Seraiki - ancient Indo-Aryan language, earlier called Lehnda, Uchi, Derawali; spoken in southern Punjab and parts of the other provinces; poets Hazrat Sachal Sarmast and Hazrat Ghulam Farid.
  • Other languages - about 75 more, including Hindko, Kashmiri, Shina, Boroshaski, Khwar, Balti, Dari, Hazargi, Potohari, Lasi and Makrani.

Key Points

  • Pakistani society is Islamic; Urdu unites all regions; agriculture is the main occupation.
  • Challenges: illiteracy, over-population, poverty, begging, drugs and child labour.
  • Literacy: 44% (1998) to 62% (2017); formal education has Primary, Secondary, Higher Secondary and Higher levels.
  • Culture = manners prevailing over ages; it reflects Islam, with shared values, festivals, architecture and calligraphy.
  • Regional cultures differ, but Islam, Urdu, customs and festivals create national solidarity.
  • Urdu means "Army"; Rahman Baba is the Sufi poet of Pashto; "Shah Jo Resalo" is the glory of Sindhi.

lessons.title: Role of Minorities in Nation Building
lessons.notes_html:
Pakistan is an Islamic country and Muslims are in the majority, so all non-Muslim citizens are collectively called "minorities". They include Christians, Hindus, Sikhs, Parsi and Qadianis etc. The minorities worked shoulder to shoulder with the Muslim leaders in the freedom movement of Pakistan, and after independence they have served the country in every field.

Quaid-e-Azam's Speech of 11th August, 1947

Just three days before independence, on 11th August, 1947, Quaid-e-Azam, addressing the Constituent Assembly of Pakistan, defined the status of minorities: "You are free; you are free to go to your temples, you are free to go to your mosques or to any other place of worship in the state of Pakistan. You may belong to any religion or caste or creed - that has nothing to do with the business of the state." He said Pakistan was starting with the fundamental principle that "we are all citizens and equal citizens of one state", with no discrimination between one community, caste or creed and another.

Rights and Representation

  • The Constitution of 1973 resolves that all citizens have equal rights and protects the rights and interests of the minorities.
  • Their quota of representation has been fixed in the federal and provincial services.
  • They enjoy religious liberty; their places of worship are protected and looked after by the Auqaf Department.
  • They are not discriminated in job opportunities in public sector departments.
  • They have due representation in the National Assembly and Senate and in the four Provincial Assemblies.

Services in the Judiciary

  • Justice A. R. Cornelius - Chief Justice of Pakistan from 1960 to 1968; his verdicts stand high in Pakistan's judicial history.
  • Justice Dorab Patel - Chief Justice of the Sindh High Court, later a justice in the Supreme Court.
  • Rana Bhagwan Das - justice in the Sindh High Court, senior judge in the Supreme Court, and Chairman, Federal Public Service Commission.

Services in Diplomacy

  • Samuel Martin Burke played an important role in the Pakistan Movement and in laying down the principles of Pakistan's foreign policy.
  • Raja Tridev Roy (Buddhist) and Jamshed Merker (Parsi) served on important diplomatic chairs; Raja Tridev Roy was appointed a lifelong federal minister for his diplomatic services.

Key Points

  • Non-Muslim citizens are called minorities; they stood shoulder to shoulder with Muslims in the freedom movement.
  • Quaid-e-Azam, 11th August 1947: freedom of worship; all are equal citizens of one state.
  • The Constitution of 1973 gives equal rights, service quotas and assembly representation to minorities.
  • Judiciary: Justice A. R. Cornelius (Chief Justice 1960-1968), Justice Dorab Patel, Rana Bhagwan Das.
  • Diplomacy: Samuel Martin Burke, Raja Tridev Roy, Jamshed Merker.
  • Defence heroes: Major General Julian Peter, Air Commodore Nazeer Latif, Squadron Leader Peter Christy.

mcqs.q: In Pakistan, all non-Muslim citizens are collectively called:
mcqs.why: Pakistan is an Islamic country and Muslims are in the majority, so all non-Muslim citizens are collectively called 'minorities' — they include Christians, Hindus, Sikhs, Parsi and Qadianis.

mcqs.q: Quaid-e-Azam's famous speech defining the status of minorities was delivered on:
mcqs.why: Just three days before independence, on 11th August, 1947, Quaid-e-Azam addressed the Constituent Assembly and said all are citizens and equal citizens of one state, free to go to their temples, mosques or any place of worship.

mcqs.q: According to the Quaid's 11th August speech, religion, caste or creed has nothing to do with:
mcqs.why: Quaid-e-Azam said: 'You may belong to any religion or caste or creed — that has nothing to do with the business of the state', and Pakistan was starting with the principle that all are equal citizens of one state.

mcqs.q: The places of worship of minorities are protected and looked after by:
mcqs.why: Minorities enjoy religious liberty; their places of worship are protected and looked after by the Auqaf Department, and the Constitution of 1973 protects their rights and interests.

mcqs.q: Justice A. R. Cornelius, a minority judge, served as Chief Justice of Pakistan from:
mcqs.why: Justice A. R. Cornelius was Chief Justice of Pakistan from 1960 to 1968 — a period of 1968 - 1960 = 8 years; his verdicts stand high in Pakistan's judicial history.

mcqs.q: Rana Bhagwan Das served as Chairman of:
mcqs.why: Rana Bhagwan Das was a justice in the Sindh High Court, a senior judge in the Supreme Court, and Chairman, Federal Public Service Commission.

mcqs.q: Who played an important role in the Pakistan Movement and in laying down the principles of Pakistan's foreign policy?
mcqs.why: In diplomacy, Samuel Martin Burke played an important role in the Pakistan Movement and in laying down the principles of Pakistan's foreign policy; Raja Tridev Roy and Jamshed Merker also served on important diplomatic chairs.

mcqs.q: Raja Tridev Roy, appointed a lifelong federal minister for his diplomatic services, belonged to which community?
mcqs.why: Raja Tridev Roy (Buddhist) and Jamshed Merker (Parsi) served on important diplomatic chairs; Raja Tridev Roy was appointed a lifelong federal minister for his diplomatic services.

mcqs.q: Air Commodore Nazeer Latif was awarded which honour twice?
mcqs.why: In defence services, Air Commodore Nazeer Latif was awarded Sitara-e-Jurat twice; Squadron Leader Peter Christy received Tamgha-e-Jurat and Sitara-e-Jurat, and Major General Julian Peter received Hilal-e-Imtiaz.

mcqs.q: Which rights does the Constitution of 1973 give to minorities?
options: Equal rights, service quotas and representation in the assemblies
mcqs.why: The Constitution of 1973 resolves that all citizens have equal rights and protects the rights and interests of minorities; they have a fixed quota in services and due representation in the National Assembly, Senate and Provincial Assemblies.
